title: Causality, infinity, and horizons
one_line_summary: Builds Penrose's conformal toolkit for the global causal structure of spacetime: conformally related metrics keep light cones intact, the five kinds of infinity of Minkowski space are pulled to a finite boundary on a patch of the Einstein static cylinder, and the resulting Penrose diagrams expose particle and event horizons in de Sitter space and spacelike Big-Bang and Big-Crunch singularities in the Robertson-Walker universes, ending with the multiple-image tour of a closed recollapsing universe.
role_in_book: Closing chapter of Part III (Cosmology). Chapters 15-18 produced a zoo of numbered model universes (Universe 1 de Sitter, Universe 6 closed dust, Universe 8 Einstein static); this chapter steps back and asks what an observer inside each of them can ever see or affect, and supplies a single graphical language for answering. The authors flag it as optional mathematics, but it is the book's first encounter with Penrose diagrams, horizons, and singularities treated as edges of spacetime. Part IV reuses exactly this language for black holes (Chapter 25, with Kruskal coordinates in Chapter 27), and Chapter 50 reopens global techniques for the Big-Bang singularity.

assumed_background.topic: Minkowski metric, spacetime interval, timelike/null/spacelike separation and light cones
Light-cone (null) coordinates u = t - x, v = t + x in flat spacetime
The metric as a machine g(x, y) taking two vectors; line elements in spherical polars
Tipping light cones in curved spacetime as a picture of causal limits
Robertson-Walker line element with curvature index k and the radial function Sigma(chi)
Hyperbolic geometry and the Poincare disc representation
Friedmann equations and cosmological redshift 1 + z = a_ob / a_em
The numbered model universes: Universe 1 (de Sitter), Universe 3 (Einstein-de Sitter), Universe 6 (closed dust), Universe 7 (open dust), Universe 8 (Einstein static)
Realising de Sitter spacetime as a hyperboloid sitting inside flat 5D Minkowski space
Trigonometric and hyperbolic identities (sec^2 = 1 + tan^2, tan addition), inverse tangent and tanh
Basic idea of topology (properties unchanged by deformation), identification of edges to make cylinders
Electromagnetic wave solutions (for the conformal-invariance exercise)

learning_objectives: Reader can state what it means for a spacetime to be time-orientable and sketch a strip of light cones that fails to be orientable once its edges are glued.
Reader can explain why a closed timelike curve would break the cause-before-effect ordering, and why ordinary timelike curves run from the remote past to the remote future.

Reader can define conformally related metrics, show that a conformal rescaling leaves angles and the null condition unchanged, and conclude that light-cone (causal) structure is conformally invariant.
Reader can name and locate the five infinities of Minkowski space (i+, i-, i0, scri+, scri-) and say which kinds of curve end on each.

Reader can carry out the compactification of Minkowski space: light-cone coordinates, arctangent squashing, removal of the divergent factor by a conformal factor, and recognition of the Einstein static metric in the new coordinates.
Reader can explain why a naive substitution V = 1/v fails and how introducing an unphysical conformally related metric rescues the construction.
Reader can read a Penrose diagram: 45-degree null lines, curves of constant r and t, boundary pieces as infinities, and the causal past of an event.
Reader can draw the Penrose diagram of de Sitter space and explain why its spacelike null infinities produce particle horizons and future event horizons that are absent in Minkowski space.
Reader can distinguish particle horizon, future event horizon and past event horizon, and classify events relative to a world line as seen, influenced, both, or neither.
Reader can introduce conformal time dt = a dtau and use it to show a Robertson-Walker spacetime is conformal to part of the Einstein static universe.
Reader can explain why the Big Bang appears as a spacelike boundary surface rather than a point, and how a singularity differs from an infinity.

Reader can narrate what an observer in a closed dust universe sees during expansion and recollapse: a growing number of sources, the whole universe at maximum expansion, duplicate images afterwards, and the shift from redshift to blueshift.

teaching_approach.summary: A picture-first, deliberately informal chapter that turns the abstract question 'where is infinity, and what can I ever see?' into a drawing exercise. The authors first point arrows at the different kinds of infinity on an ordinary t-r diagram, promise that these can be squashed to a finite boundary, and show the finished Penrose triangle before doing any algebra. Only then do they build the map, including a deliberately failed first attempt, and they reuse one reference geometry, the Einstein static cylinder, as a common canvas onto which Minkowski, de Sitter and Robertson-Walker spacetimes are painted as patches. Horizons and singularities are then read directly off the shapes of those patches, and the chapter ends with a narrative tour of a closed universe told through the diagram.
narrative_arc: Motivating question: can we say, for any model universe, which events can influence which, and whether waiting long enough lets an observer hear from everywhere?
Local preliminaries: time orientation of light cones, causality as cause-in-the-past-light-cone, and closed timelike curves as the only loophole.
Tool: conformally related metrics preserve angles and null directions, so they preserve causal structure while discarding distances (Poincare disc as a familiar example).
Intuitive catalogue: five arrows on a Minkowski t-r plot for the five kinds of infinity, followed immediately by the finished Penrose triangle.
Reading the diagram: where constant-r and constant-t lines go, null rays stay at 45 degrees, and an observer in Minkowski space eventually receives signals from every particle.

Formalism: light-cone coordinates, a failed 1/v substitution, the unphysical-metric fix, then the arctangent map that turns Minkowski into a bounded patch of the Einstein static universe, with coordinates of i+, i0, i- and the null boundary lines.
Application 1: de Sitter space is conformal to a finite time-strip of the Einstein cylinder, so its null infinities are spacelike; this produces particle horizons and future and past event horizons.
Application 2: Robertson-Walker spacetimes via conformal time map to regions whose lower edge is the Big Bang, a spacelike singular surface; closed k = 1 adds a Big-Crunch surface.
Narrative check: an observer's view of a closed universe through expansion and collapse, including duplicate images and redshift turning to blueshift.
Wrap-up: singularities are boundaries of spacetime at finite distance, infinities are boundaries at infinite distance; pointer to black holes and to the final chapter.
signature_moves: Shows the answer diagram (Fig. 19.5b) before deriving the map, with a margin note promising the mathematics later, so the algebra has a target.
Stages a failed attempt (V = 1/v makes the line element blow up) to motivate why a conformal factor and an 'unphysical' metric are needed.
Uses the arctangent graph as the single visual idea behind compactification.
Treats the Einstein static cylinder as a universal backdrop: every spacetime in the chapter is drawn as a shaded patch on it before being flattened into a Penrose diagram.
Reads physics (horizons, what can be seen) straight off boundary shapes: a point-like i- means no particle horizon, a spacelike scri- or Big-Bang line means there is one.
Offers a mnemonic for event horizons: stand at future infinity and look back for the future horizon, stand at past infinity and look forward for the past horizon.
Classifies spacetime regions around a world line into seen-and-influenced, influenced-only and seen-only (Fig. 19.17).
Ends with a vivid closed-universe story (all stars at maximum expansion, duplicates afterwards, glimpsing the back of your own head at the Crunch) and pairs it with a red/blueshift account.
Pushes key computations (angle invariance, de Sitter compactification, coordinate relations, Coleman's cycloid parametrization) into exercises.

sections.title: Chapter opening: causal structure, time orientation and the question of infinity
sections.summary: Announces the aim of understanding the causal structure of the model universes. Defines time-orientability as the ability to split all non-spacelike vectors consistently into future- and past-pointing ones, illustrated by cones on a strip that is glued into a cylinder with or without a twist, and suggests entropy increase as a practical arrow. States the causality rule that causes must lie in the past light cone of their effects, notes that closed timelike loops are the one way to violate it (with the familiar ancestor-killing paradox), and says such loops are rare. Then poses the global questions: what does a signal from infinitely far away mean, and are there regions we can never contact even in principle? Introduces the horizon-on-the-skyline image, credits Penrose's 1960s conformal toolkit, and previews Penrose diagrams as two-dimensional cartoons with infinities at the edges and light at 45 degrees. A boxed note says the chapter can be skipped on first reading.
key_moves: Time orientation is a global consistency condition, not a local one: locally every cone looks fine, but gluing a strip with a twist destroys a global future direction.
Causality is phrased entirely through light cones, so anything that preserves light cones preserves causal relations.
Closed timelike curves are the only way a particle can stay inside its own forward cones yet revisit its past.
Frames infinity as limiting behaviour of timelike, null and spacelike curves, and horizons as boundaries of what can be accessed.

sections.title: Penrose diagrams
sections.summary: Introduces conformally related metrics, g-hat = Omega^2 g, and shows that ratios of inner products, hence angles and the vanishing of null norms, are unchanged, so both metrics share one light-cone structure. Example 19.1 uses the Poincare disc (inspired by Escher) as a familiar conformal picture in which angles survive but sizes shrink toward the boundary. Then works intuitively on a Minkowski t-r half-plane: identifies future and past timelike infinity i+ and i-, spacelike infinity i0, and future and past null infinity scri+ and scri-, and asserts that a conformal map squeezes all of Minkowski space into a shaded triangle whose edges are those infinities. Describes how vertical (constant-r) lines become curves from i- to i+, horizontal (constant-t) lines become curves ending at i0, and null rays stay at 45 degrees, reflecting through r' = 0 and running from scri- to scri+. Example 19.2 shows that the causal past of any event eventually includes i-, so a Minkowski observer can in principle receive light from every particle.
concepts: conformal invariance of the light-cone structure
key_moves: Ratio of two metric inner products is independent of Omega, so cosines of angles and nullness are conformal invariants.
Five distinct limits: t to +/- infinity at fixed r, r to infinity at fixed t, and t +/- r to infinity along light rays.
Points versus surfaces: timelike and spacelike infinities compress to points, null infinities to 45-degree edges.
Every timelike geodesic starts at i- and ends at i+; every spacelike one begins and ends at i0; every null geodesic goes from scri- to scri+.
Because every world line starts at i-, no Minkowski particle is permanently hidden from an observer who waits.

sections.title: Penrose diagrams (continued): compactifying Minkowski space onto the Einstein cylinder
sections.summary: Makes the map explicit through Examples 19.3-19.6. Rewrites Minkowski space in light-cone coordinates u = t - r, v = t + r, where outgoing rays have constant u and incoming rays constant v, and each point of the u-v plot stands for a 2-sphere. Tries V = 1/v to bring v = infinity to V = 0, finds the line element blows up, and fixes this by multiplying by V^2 to get an unphysical but conformally related metric that is regular at V = 0. Repeats the idea more cleverly with Omega^2 = 4/[(1+u^2)(1+v^2)] and u = tan q, v = tan p, finds the rescaled line element -4 dp dq + sin^2(p-q) dOmega^2, and with t' = p + q, r' = p - q recognises the Einstein static universe (Universe 8). Draws the Einstein universe as a cylinder of 3-spheres, shows Minkowski space as a bounded shaded patch on it, and in Example 19.6 identifies i0 = (0, pi), i+ = (pi, 0), i- = (-pi, 0) and the null lines t' + r' = pi and t' - r' = -pi as scri+ and scri-. A closing paragraph points to global techniques for singularity arguments.
key_moves: Suppress the 2-sphere factor so a 2D diagram suffices, remembering each point is a sphere.
A coordinate change alone cannot put infinity at a finite place without making the metric singular there; a conformal factor that vanishes at infinity cancels the divergence.
Squash with arctangent so the whole real line becomes a finite interval, then choose Omega to absorb the sec^2 factors.
The rescaled metric is not Minkowski but the Einstein static universe, so Minkowski space becomes a finite region of a larger, well-understood spacetime whose boundary is Minkowski's infinity.
Coordinates of the boundary pieces follow from t' +/- r' = 2 arctan(t +/- r).

sections.title: The de Sitter spacetime
sections.summary: Takes Universe 1 (exponentially expanding flat slices) and asserts, with details left to an exercise via the hyperboloid embedding, that its metric equals alpha^2 sec^2 t' times the Einstein static metric for -pi/2 < t' < pi/2, with alpha = 1/H. The Penrose diagram is therefore a square: no point-like i+, i- or i0, but horizontal edges scri- and scri+ that are spacelike, each spanning all chi at a single conformal instant. Because world lines begin on a spacelike scri-, the past light cone of an event need not catch every world line, which opens the door to horizons.
key_moves: Conformal factor sec^2 t' diverges at t' = +/- pi/2, so the whole infinite de Sitter history fits in a finite strip of the cylinder.
Shape determines physics: a spacelike past boundary means past light cones have limited reach.

sections.title: The de Sitter spacetime (continued): particle horizons and event horizons
sections.summary: Defines the particle horizon at an event P as the division between comoving world lines that intersect P's past light cone and those that do not; it grows as the observer ages, so it is observer and time dependent. Shows that even when a de Sitter observer reaches scri+, the past light cone does not cover all of spacetime (Fig. 19.15): the boundary of what is ever seen is the future event horizon, which Minkowski space lacks. Example 19.7 follows a second world line Q that crosses the observer's event horizon at R; the observer never sees anything on Q after R and sees R itself only in the infinite future. Defines the past event horizon as the forward light cone from the observer's starting point on scri-, and Example 19.8 splits spacetime around a world line into regions that can be seen and influenced, influenced but never seen, and seen but never influenced.
concepts: causal regions of a world line
key_moves: Particle horizon: about world lines (which particles have ever been seen); event horizon: about events (which events will ever be seen).
Future event horizon is the past light cone of the observer's endpoint on scri+.
Past event horizon is the future light cone of the observer's starting point on scri-.
Minkowski has no event horizon because the observer's endpoint i+ has every event in its past.

sections.title: Big-Bang singularities
sections.summary: Writes the Robertson-Walker metric with Sigma(chi) = sin chi, chi, sinh chi and anticipates that the Big Bang at a = 0 will bound the image on the Einstein cylinder. Introduces conformal time through dt = a(t) dtau so that the metric becomes a^2 times a static metric. Example 19.9 treats pressure-free, Lambda = 0 models: for k = 1 the static metric is the Einstein universe itself, for k = 0 it is Minkowski restricted to positive time, and for k = -1 a tanh-arctan transformation gives a smaller triangular region; Fig. 19.18 shows the three patches on cylinders. The Penrose diagrams (Figs 19.19, 19.20) have the Big Bang as a spacelike singular surface at t' = 0, drawn as a double line. For k = 0 and k = -1 the diagram looks like the top half of Minkowski's, with world lines ending at i+, no future event horizon but a particle horizon; for k = 1 there is also a Big-Crunch surface on top, and past and future event horizons as in de Sitter.
key_moves: Conformal time strips the scale factor out as an overall conformal factor, so the causal structure of an expanding universe equals that of a static one.
The finite past (a = 0 at t = 0) cuts the image off along a horizontal, hence spacelike, line.
Different k give different patch shapes on the same Einstein cylinder.

sections.title: Big-Bang singularities (continued): a tour of the closed Universe 6 and singularities as boundaries
sections.summary: Example 19.10 follows an observer in the closed dust model through its life. Treating the chi direction as a closed loop, the observer's past light cone takes in more and more sources as the universe expands, reaches every source at maximum expansion (light arriving both ways around the loop), then, during contraction, begins to deliver second images of distant sources that come the long way round. Light from the observer's own location just after the Bang would complete the circuit exactly at the Crunch, so nothing can ever circle the universe. Early light is redshifted; during collapse the direct image of a source can be blueshifted while its long-way image is redshifted, and finally most light is blueshifted. The section concludes that singularities, like infinities, are boundaries of spacetime but can lie a finite interval away, points to black-hole Penrose diagrams in Chapter 25, and defers the question of which universe we inhabit to Chapter 50.
key_moves: In a closed universe, light-cone growth continues through recollapse, so new images keep appearing.
Each shift is set by comparing a at emission and at observation, which explains redshift then blueshift.
Timing coincidence: a full circuit of light takes the entire lifetime of the closed dust universe.

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: Three-point summary: conformal structure turns infinities into edge points and surfaces; Penrose diagrams display that structure and reveal horizons; singularities appear as edges that may be a finite interval away. Eight exercises cover light-cone coordinates and velocities, conformal invariance of angles and null curves, the global de Sitter compactification via the hyperboloid, conformal invariance of electromagnetism and redshift, the explicit Minkowski compactification, drawing geodesics on the Penrose triangle, and Coleman's cycloid treatment of the closed dust universe.
concepts: cycloid parametrization of the closed dust universe
key_moves: Exercises fill in the derivations the text asserts (19.23, the t'-r' relation, the Universe 6 timing).

concepts.name: causal structure
concepts.definition: The pattern of which events can influence which others in a spacetime, fixed by the arrangement of light cones at every event together with a choice of future direction; two spacetimes with the same null cones everywhere have the same causal relations.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced in the opening paragraph as the organising question for all the model universes of Part III, then made operational by insisting that the comparison tool must preserve light cones.
concepts.notes: The chapter never gives a formal definition (causal past/future sets J^-(p), J^+(p)); a tutor may want to add them.

concepts.name: time orientability
concepts.definition: A spacetime is time-orientable if a continuous choice of 'future' half of the light cone can be made at every event, so that every timelike or null vector is consistently classified as future- or past-pointing across the whole manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with flat space where one cone suffices; Fig. 19.1(b,c) shows a strip of cones glued into a cylinder, once with all cones upright (orientable) and once with cones rotating across the strip so the gluing swaps future and past (non-orientable). Entropy growth is offered as a practical way to pick the future.
concepts.notes: The book writes 'orientable' in the figure caption; strictly this is time-orientability, which is distinct from spatial orientability.

concepts.name: causality
concepts.definition: Cause must come before effect and be joined to it by a timelike or null separation, so the events a particle can affect lie within its future light cone and the events that can affect it lie within its past light cone.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated from the no-faster-than-light rule, then extended to curved spacetime by recalling from Chapter 5 that local light cones along a world line encode the limits.

concepts.name: closed timelike curve
concepts.definition: A timelike world line that returns to an event it has already passed through, so that an observer always moving into its local future cone nonetheless revisits its own past, permitting causal paradoxes.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as the only way causality could fail, illustrated by a loop threaded through tilted light cones (Fig. 19.2) and the grandfather-type paradox; a footnote says some black-hole interiors contain them.
concepts.notes: Book does not name examples beyond the black-hole remark; Kerr interior (Chapter 29) and Godel universe are standard cases.

concepts.name: light cone
concepts.definition: At each event, the set of directions (tangent vectors) with zero spacetime interval; it separates timelike directions inside from spacelike directions outside and bounds the events that light signals can reach or come from.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from earlier chapters as the carrier of causal information; the whole chapter is built on keeping these cones at 45 degrees on diagrams.

concepts.name: conformally related metrics
concepts.definition: Two metrics on the same manifold are conformally related if one is a positive smooth function times the other at every point, g-hat(x) = Omega(x)^2 g(x); the rescaling changes lengths and curvature but not angles or null directions.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated as the comparison tool that keeps light cones intact; defined by eqn 19.1 and immediately shown to preserve ratios of inner products (19.2).
concepts.notes: Distinguish from a conformal coordinate transformation (a diffeomorphism): here the manifold and coordinates are fixed and the metric itself is replaced.

concepts.name: conformal factor
concepts.definition: The positive function Omega(x) (or its square) relating conformally related metrics; in compactification it is chosen to vanish at infinity so that the rescaled metric stays finite there.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in eqn 19.1, then chosen concretely as Omega = V in Example 19.4 and Omega^2 = 4/[(1+u^2)(1+v^2)] in Example 19.5; later a^2(t) and alpha^2 sec^2 t' play the same role for cosmologies.
concepts.notes: The book writes ds^2 = (1/Omega^2) d-bar-s^2 in places and ds^2 = a^2 d-bar-s^2 in others; the factor's direction (physical over unphysical or the reverse) switches between examples.

concepts.name: conformal invariance of the light-cone structure
aliases: conformal invariance of angles and null vectors
concepts.definition: Under g -> Omega^2 g the cosine of the angle between any two vectors and the ratio of any two inner products are unchanged, so null vectors remain null, timelike remain timelike, and the causal relations between events are identical.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived in one line from eqn 19.2 using the metric-based angle formula in a margin note (19.3); the proof is set as Exercise 19.3.
concepts.notes: Null geodesics stay null geodesics (as unparametrised curves) under conformal rescaling; timelike geodesics generally do not stay geodesics, a point the book does not raise.

concepts.name: conformal structure
concepts.definition: The equivalence class of a metric under conformal rescaling: what remains of the geometry once overall local scale is forgotten, namely angles and the light-cone (causal) structure.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as Penrose's way to strip away 'geometrical baggage' and compare universes by the arrangement of their light cones; the Penrose diagram is its picture.

concepts.name: conformal compactification
aliases: mapping infinity to a finite boundary
concepts.definition: The procedure of choosing coordinates in which infinite coordinate ranges become finite, and a conformal factor that vanishes at infinity, so that the rescaled (unphysical) metric extends smoothly to include the points at infinity as a boundary with the same causal structure as the original spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Laid out as a two-step strategy after the failed V = 1/v attempt: map infinity to finite coordinates, then pass to a conformally related metric free of coordinate trouble; executed fully for Minkowski space in Example 19.5.
concepts.notes: The explicit relation between (t, r) and (t', r') is left to Exercise 19.6; the answer appears in Appendix E.

concepts.name: unphysical metric
concepts.definition: A metric conformally related to the physical one, g-bar = Omega^2 g, used only as a device: it is regular where the physical metric's infinity lies, so the boundary can be studied, and it has the same light cones though different distances and curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Coined in Example 19.4 as a 'sidestep' after substituting V = 1/v leaves Minkowski singular at V = 0; multiplying by V^2 gives a line element well behaved there.
concepts.notes: The unphysical metric for Minkowski turns out to be the Einstein static universe, which is curved; learners should not think the rescaled metric is still flat.

concepts.name: Penrose diagram
concepts.definition: A two-dimensional drawing of a conformally compactified spacetime (angular directions suppressed) in which radial light rays run at 45 degrees, the whole infinite spacetime fits in a finite region, and the edges of that region are the infinities and singularities; distances are distorted but causal relations are faithful.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed as a cartoon of infinities in the opening, shown in finished form for Minkowski space (Fig. 19.5b) before derivation, then built from the Einstein cylinder patch and applied to de Sitter and Robertson-Walker spacetimes.
concepts.notes: Each point of the diagram stands for a 2-sphere (except points on the r = 0 axis). Reappears for black holes in GA ch25-ch27.

concepts.name: future timelike infinity
concepts.definition: The idealised endpoint reached by timelike curves as proper time goes to plus infinity; in the Minkowski Penrose diagram it is the single top vertex at (t', r') = (pi, 0).
concepts.how_introduced: First as an arrow pointing up the t axis ('where do we end up if we wait forever here?'), then as a vertex of the triangle, then with coordinates in Example 19.6.
concepts.notes: Absent as a point in de Sitter space, where timelike curves end on a spacelike scri+.

concepts.name: past timelike infinity
concepts.definition: The idealised starting point of timelike curves as proper time goes to minus infinity; for Minkowski space the bottom vertex (t', r') = (-pi, 0).
concepts.how_introduced: Down-pointing arrows in Fig. 19.5(a), noting that flat space has no Big Bang so world lines extend forever into the past.

concepts.name: spacelike infinity
concepts.definition: The idealised limit of spacelike curves as distance goes to infinity at finite time; in the Minkowski diagram the right-hand vertex (t', r') = (0, pi), where all constant-t slices end.
concepts.how_introduced: Arrows pointing out along r in Fig. 19.5(a); noted to be causally disconnected from the observer.
concepts.notes: Fig. 19.19 also labels a vertex i0 for flat and open Robertson-Walker models.

concepts.name: future null infinity
concepts.definition: The boundary surface where outgoing light rays end as their affine parameter goes to infinity; in Minkowski space the null edge t' + r' = pi of the Penrose triangle, in de Sitter space a spacelike edge t' = pi/2.
concepts.how_introduced: Diagonal arrows in Fig. 19.5(a) for light sent outward; then the upper edge of the triangle; located as a line in Example 19.6.
concepts.notes: Margin note gives the spoken name 'scri plus'. The OCR copy sometimes renders it as J^+.

concepts.name: past null infinity
concepts.definition: The boundary surface from which incoming light rays originate; in Minkowski space the null edge t' - r' = -pi, in de Sitter a spacelike edge t' = -pi/2.
concepts.how_introduced: Arrows for light arriving from far away in Fig. 19.5(a); lower edge of the triangle; line equation in Example 19.6.
concepts.notes: In Figs 19.19-19.21 the book also labels the Big-Bang singular surface 'scri-', which is nonstandard (see gaps).

concepts.name: light-cone coordinates
aliases: retarded and advanced time u, v
concepts.definition: Coordinates u = t - r and v = t + r adapted to radial light rays: outgoing rays have constant u, incoming rays constant v, and the radial part of the Minkowski line element becomes -du dv.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 19.3 converts Minkowski space to spherical polars and then to u, v as the first step toward compactification; Fig. 19.9 shows the grid of constant-u and constant-v lines. Exercises 19.1-19.2 revisit them in 1+1 dimensions.
formulas: u = t - r,\; v = t + r
concepts.notes: Exercise 19.2 shows the 'light-cone velocity' du/dv = (1-beta)/(1+beta) behaves oddly, a warning about coordinate speeds.

concepts.name: arctangent compactification
aliases: u = tan q, v = tan p substitution
concepts.definition: Using y = arctan x to map the entire real line, including plus and minus infinity as limits, onto the finite interval from -pi/2 to pi/2, applied separately to each null coordinate so the infinite null plane becomes a finite square.
concepts.how_introduced: Fig. 19.10 graphs arctan with its horizontal asymptotes as the key idea; Example 19.5 sets v = tan p, u = tan q.
formulas: v = \tan p,\; u = \tan q,\; -\pi/2 < p, q < \pi/2
concepts.notes: Any monotone map with finite asymptotes (e.g. tanh) would do; the arctan choice is what makes the result the Einstein static metric.

concepts.name: Einstein static universe
concepts.definition: The static closed (k = 1) cosmology whose spatial sections are unchanging 3-spheres, line element -dt^2 + dchi^2 + sin^2 chi dOmega^2 with 0 <= chi <= pi; with two angular dimensions suppressed it is drawn as an infinite cylinder, and it serves as the common arena into which other spacetimes are conformally embedded.
concepts.how_introduced: Recognised unexpectedly as the rescaled metric at the end of Example 19.5; drawn as a cylinder of circles (Fig. 19.11) and then used as the backdrop on which Minkowski (Fig. 19.12), de Sitter and Robertson-Walker patches (Fig. 19.18) are painted.
concepts.notes: Embedding as a cylinder in higher-dimensional Minkowski space is sketched in a margin note with a pointer to Appendix D. Its physical instability (Chapter 18) is irrelevant here: it is used only as a conformal canvas.

concepts.name: topology of a spacetime manifold
concepts.definition: The properties of the spacetime manifold that survive continuous deformation, such as whether spatial sections are closed and how the manifold is glued; for the Einstein universe it is a line of time times a 3-sphere, drawn as a cylinder.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned as what conformal structure lets one focus on, with a boxed pointer to Appendix C; used concretely for the Einstein cylinder and for identifying edges in Fig. 19.1.

concepts.name: Poincare disc
aliases: Poincare disc model of the hyperbolic plane
concepts.definition: A map of the infinite hyperbolic (Lobachevskian) plane into the interior of a unit disc that preserves angles; geodesics appear as arcs meeting the boundary circle at right angles and congruent figures shrink toward the rim, which represents infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 19.1 recalls hyperbolic geometry (triangle angles sum below pi) and shows an Escher-inspired triangle tiling (Fig. 19.3) as a conformal representation in which every triangle is equivalent despite looking smaller near the edge.
formulas: ds^2 = \frac{4(dx^2+dy^2)}{(1-x^2-y^2)^2} (standard form, not in the book)
concepts.notes: It is a direct Riemannian analogue of a Penrose diagram: infinity on a finite rim, angles kept, sizes not. The book does not make this link explicitly.

concepts.name: de Sitter spacetime
concepts.definition: The vacuum-energy-dominated solution with constant Hubble rate H = sqrt(Lambda/3); in flat slicing ds^2 = -dt^2 + e^{2Ht}(dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2), and globally it is a hyperboloid in five-dimensional Minkowski space, conformal to the strip -pi/2 < t' < pi/2 of the Einstein static universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Picked as the first test case after Minkowski; the conformal relation 19.23 is asserted with the derivation delegated to Exercise 19.4, and its square Penrose diagram (Fig. 19.13) is read for horizons.
formulas: ds^2 = \alpha^2 \sec^2 t'\, d\bar s^2_{\rm Einstein},\; \alpha = 1/H,\; -\pi/2 < t' < \pi/2
concepts.notes: The flat-slicing coordinates of eqn 19.22 cover only half of the square diagram; the conformal relation holds for the global (cosh) coordinates of Exercise 19.4(b).

concepts.name: spacelike conformal boundary
concepts.definition: A piece of conformal infinity (such as scri+ or scri- in de Sitter space) that is a spacelike surface in the compactified spacetime rather than a null one; its presence is what produces horizons.
concepts.how_introduced: Noted as the striking difference between de Sitter's square diagram and Minkowski's triangle: the null infinities become horizontal lines spanning all chi at one conformal time.
concepts.notes: Standard rule of thumb (Rindler, Penrose): spacelike scri- gives particle horizons, spacelike scri+ gives event horizons. The book shows this through examples rather than stating it.

concepts.name: particle horizon
concepts.definition: For an observer at event P, the boundary between the world lines of comoving particles that intersect P's past light cone (particles that have been seen at least once) and those that do not; it exists when the past boundary of spacetime is spacelike and it grows as the observer ages.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown pictorially in Fig. 19.14 with world lines rising from a spacelike scri- and a past cone from P catching only some of them; then applied to Robertson-Walker models in Section 19.3.
formulas: \chi_{\rm ph}(\tau) = \tau - \tau_{\rm initial} (comoving radius in conformal time; standard, not in the book)
concepts.notes: Absent in Minkowski space because every world line starts at the point i-, which lies in every causal past.

concepts.name: future event horizon
concepts.definition: For an observer's world line, the past light cone of its endpoint on future infinity: the boundary of the set of events that will ever be seen by that observer, however long they wait.
concepts.how_introduced: Found in de Sitter space by noting that when the observer reaches the spacelike scri+ their past cone still leaves part of spacetime unseen (Fig. 19.15, 19.16); Example 19.7 shows another particle's history freezing at the crossing point R.
concepts.notes: Minkowski and flat or open dust universes have none, because world lines end at a point i+ whose past contains everything; de Sitter and closed k = 1 universes have one. Direct precursor of the black-hole event horizon.

concepts.name: past event horizon
concepts.definition: For an observer's world line, the future light cone of its starting point on past infinity: the boundary of the set of events that the observer can ever influence.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by symmetry with the future event horizon on p.211, with a margin mnemonic (sit at future infinity and look back; sit at past infinity and look forward) and Fig. 19.17.
concepts.notes: The book also says flat and open dust universes have a past event horizon; in their case the observer's world line starts on the Big-Bang surface, so this is really a statement about the limited causal future of an early event, and most texts would not use this name there.

concepts.name: observer dependence of horizons
concepts.definition: Cosmological particle and event horizons are defined relative to a chosen observer's world line (and, for the particle horizon, a moment on it), not as fixed places in spacetime; different observers have different horizons.
concepts.how_introduced: Remarked when the particle horizon is seen to widen as the observer moves up the world line, and implicit in the construction of horizons from each observer's endpoints.
concepts.notes: Contrast later with black-hole event horizons, which are defined relative to all of future null infinity and so are observer independent.

concepts.name: causal regions of a world line
aliases: causal past and future of a world line
concepts.definition: The partition of spacetime relative to a whole world line into events that are both in its causal past and future (seen and influenced), only in its causal future (influenced, never seen), only in its causal past (seen, never influenced), and in neither.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 19.8 labels regions I, II and III on a de Sitter-like rectangle crossed by the past and future event horizons of a vertical world line W (Fig. 19.17).
concepts.notes: The fourth region (the side triangles, neither seen nor influenced) is drawn but not named in the book.

concepts.name: causal past of an event
concepts.definition: The set of all events from which a signal travelling at or below light speed can reach a given event P; on a Penrose diagram it is the region below P bounded by the two 45-degree lines through P.
concepts.how_introduced: Shaded in Fig. 19.8 for a point P in Minkowski space (Example 19.2) and used to argue that eventually every particle becomes visible.

concepts.name: conformal time
concepts.definition: A time coordinate tau defined by dt = a(t) dtau, in which the Robertson-Walker line element becomes a(t)^2 times a static metric, so radial light rays obey dchi = +/- dtau and travel at 45 degrees.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced in Section 19.3 as the step that lets expanding universes be compared with the Einstein static cylinder; Exercise 19.8 identifies it with the comoving distance a light ray covers.
concepts.notes: The finite or infinite range of tau decides the shape of the diagram. For closed dust it runs from 0 to 2 pi, not 0 to infinity as Example 19.9 says (see gaps).

concepts.name: Robertson-Walker spacetime
concepts.definition: The homogeneous isotropic cosmological metric ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2[dchi^2 + Sigma(chi)^2 dOmega^2] with Sigma = sin chi, chi, sinh chi for k = +1, 0, -1; every such spacetime is conformally flat, and via conformal time it maps onto part of the Einstein static universe.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 16 in Section 19.3, then rewritten with conformal time and mapped for the pressure-free Lambda = 0 cases in Example 19.9.

concepts.name: spacelike singularity
concepts.definition: A singularity that forms a spacelike boundary of spacetime, reached by all world lines at (or from) a single moment rather than at a location one could avoid; in Robertson-Walker Penrose diagrams the Big Bang is the horizontal line t' = 0, drawn doubled.
concepts.how_introduced: Predicted because a(0) = 0 must cut off the Einstein-cylinder image; then read from the bottom edge of Figs 19.19 and 19.20, from which every world line starts.
concepts.notes: Sets up the spacelike singularity at r = 0 inside Schwarzschild black holes in Part IV.

concepts.name: Big Crunch
concepts.definition: The future singularity of a recollapsing closed universe where the scale factor returns to zero; in its Penrose diagram it is a second spacelike singular line along the top edge.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears as the upper double line in the k = 1 Penrose diagram (Fig. 19.20) and as the climax of the Universe 6 tour in Example 19.10.

concepts.name: closed universe multiple images
concepts.definition: In a spatially closed universe a source can be seen along more than one light path, for example the short way and the long way around a great circle, so an observer may receive several images of the same object emitted at different epochs.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 19.10 follows the observer's growing past light cone on the k = 1 diagram with the chi direction treated as periodic (Fig. 19.21) and on a circle picture of space (Fig. 19.22).
concepts.notes: The book's square diagram with chi = 0 identified with chi = pi is a rescaled picture of one great circle; in true 3-sphere coordinates chi = 0 and chi = pi are antipodes and the conformal lifetime is 2 pi.

concepts.name: cosmological redshift and blueshift
concepts.definition: Light received from an emitter has its frequency scaled by a(t_em)/a(t_ob): redshifted if the universe has grown since emission, blueshifted if it has shrunk.
concepts.how_introduced: Used at the end of Example 19.10 to narrate the switch from red to blue during recollapse, and derived in Exercise 19.5 from conformal invariance of electromagnetism.

concepts.name: conformal invariance of electromagnetism
concepts.definition: In four dimensions the Maxwell action and field equations are unchanged by a conformal rescaling of the metric, so electromagnetic waves in a conformally flat spacetime are simply the flat-space waves in conformal coordinates.
concepts.how_introduced: Only in Exercise 19.5, where it gives the redshift law omega a = const for a Robertson-Walker universe.

concepts.name: singularity versus infinity
concepts.definition: In the conformal picture both infinities and singularities are edges of spacetime, but an infinity lies at infinite interval from any observer while a singularity can be reached, or have come from, a finite proper time away; physics breaks down at a singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn as the concluding lesson of Section 19.3 and restated in the chapter summary.

concepts.name: conformal structure of infinity
concepts.definition: The boundary added to a spacetime by conformal compactification, together with its causal character (null, spacelike, or point-like pieces), which encodes how curves of each type end.
concepts.how_introduced: Named when Minkowski space is seen to occupy only a limited region of the Einstein cylinder, so that the edge of that region represents its infinity (Fig. 19.12).

concepts.name: global techniques
concepts.definition: Methods that analyse spacetime as a whole (causal structure, conformal boundaries, topology) rather than through local field equations, used for example to prove singularity theorems.
concepts.how_introduced: One-sentence forward pointer at the end of Section 19.1 to Chapter 50 and to Penrose (1973).

concepts.name: cycloid parametrization of the closed dust universe
concepts.definition: Writing the closed, pressure-free, Lambda = 0 Friedmann solution in terms of conformal time: a = (C/2)(1 - cos eta), t = (C/2)(eta - sin eta), so the universe lasts from eta = 0 to eta = 2 pi.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 19.8, credited to Sidney Coleman, asks the reader to derive it and use it to check the story of Example 19.10.
concepts.notes: It resolves the time ranges: maximum expansion at eta = pi, crunch at eta = 2 pi, exactly the time for light to go once round the 3-sphere.

concepts.name: hyperbolic geometry
concepts.definition: Non-Euclidean geometry of constant negative curvature in which the parallel postulate fails, triangle angles sum to less than pi, and parallel geodesics diverge.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in Example 19.1 only to motivate the Poincare disc picture.

concepts.name: horizon
concepts.definition: Generically, a surface in spacetime separating events an observer can in principle exchange signals with from those they cannot; made precise in the chapter as particle and event horizons.
concepts.how_introduced: Opened with the everyday image of the skyline horizon dividing what can and cannot be seen.

concepts.name: infinity (as limiting behaviour of curves)
concepts.definition: In this chapter infinity means the limiting region approached along an unbounded curve through spacetime; which kind of infinity is reached depends on whether the curve is timelike, null or spacelike.
concepts.how_introduced: Set in bold on p.202 when the authors ask what receiving a signal from infinitely far away would mean and whether waiting forever lets us hear from everywhere; the answer is then organised into the five Minkowski infinities.
concepts.notes: Tutor tip: stress that the infinities are not events in the physical spacetime; they are boundary points added by the compactification.

concepts.name: anthropic principle
concepts.definition: The argument that the conditions we observe must allow observers to exist, since otherwise we would not be here to observe them.
concepts.how_introduced: Only in the Brandon Carter margin note, which says Carter coined the name and quotes Penrose's tongue-in-cheek explanation of it.
concepts.notes: Aside with no role in the physics of the chapter.

key_equations.name: Conformally related metrics
key_equations.meaning: Defines when two metrics share a conformal structure: one is a smooth positive multiple of the other at each event.
key_equations.symbols: g, g-hat metrics; Omega(x) conformal factor

key_equations.name: Invariance of inner-product ratios
key_equations.latex: \frac{\hat{\boldsymbol g}(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)}{\hat{\boldsymbol g}(\boldsymbol v,\boldsymbol w)} = \frac{\boldsymbol g(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)}{\boldsymbol g(\boldsymbol v,\boldsymbol w)}
key_equations.meaning: The conformal factor cancels in any ratio of inner products at the same point, so angles, relative magnitudes and nullness are unchanged; hence light cones coincide.
key_equations.symbols: x, y, v, w arbitrary vectors at one event

key_equations.name: Metric definition of the cosine of an angle
key_equations.latex: \cos\theta = \frac{\boldsymbol g(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)}{|\boldsymbol g(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol x)\,\boldsymbol g(\boldsymbol y,\boldsymbol y)|^{1/2}}
key_equations.meaning: Angle between two non-null vectors defined from the metric; manifestly unchanged by g -> Omega^2 g.

key_equations.name: Minkowski line element, Cartesian
key_equations.meaning: Starting point of the compactification.

key_equations.name: Minkowski line element, spherical polars
key_equations.meaning: Radial form that allows suppressing the 2-sphere.

key_equations.name: Light-cone coordinates
key_equations.latex: u = t - r, \quad v = t + r
key_equations.meaning: Outgoing radial light rays have constant u, incoming ones constant v.
key_equations.symbols: u retarded time, v advanced time

key_equations.name: Minkowski metric in light-cone coordinates
key_equations.meaning: The radial-temporal part is purely off-diagonal and the sphere radius is r = (v - u)/2.

key_equations.name: Failed substitution V = 1/v
key_equations.meaning: Bringing v = infinity to V = 0 by a coordinate change alone leaves the (still Minkowski) line element divergent at V = 0.

key_equations.name: Unphysical metric defined
key_equations.meaning: Introduces a conformally related metric with Omega = V that absorbs the divergence.
key_equations.symbols: eta Minkowski metric; g-bar unphysical metric

key_equations.name: Regular unphysical line element
key_equations.meaning: The rescaled metric is finite at V = 0, so points at v = infinity can be added as a boundary.

key_equations.name: Compactifying conformal factor
key_equations.meaning: Conformal factor that vanishes as u or v goes to infinity, chosen to cancel the sec^2 factors from the arctan substitution.

key_equations.name: Arctangent substitution
key_equations.meaning: Maps each infinite null coordinate to a finite angle-like range.

key_equations.name: Range of compact null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Finite ranges; p >= q encodes r >= 0.

key_equations.name: Minkowski metric in (p, q)
key_equations.meaning: All divergence at p, q = +/- pi/2 is in the overall factor 1/Omega^2; the bracket is regular. Uses sec^2 = 1 + tan^2 and tan p - tan q = sin(p-q)/(cos p cos q).

key_equations.name: Unphysical line element in (p, q)
key_equations.meaning: The regular metric sharing Minkowski's causal structure.

key_equations.name: Compactified time and radius
key_equations.latex: t' = p + q, \quad r' = p - q
key_equations.meaning: Recombines null coordinates into timelike and spacelike ones; equivalently t' +/- r' = 2 arctan(t +/- r).

key_equations.name: Minkowski image region
key_equations.meaning: All of Minkowski space occupies a bounded triangle in the (t', r') plane.

key_equations.name: Rescaled Minkowski = Einstein static form
key_equations.meaning: The conformally rescaled Minkowski metric is the Einstein static universe restricted to the triangle (19.17).

key_equations.name: Einstein static universe (Universe 8)
key_equations.meaning: Static closed cosmology of unit radius; the reference canvas of the chapter.

key_equations.name: 3-sphere coordinate ranges
key_equations.meaning: Coordinates covering each spatial 3-sphere of the Einstein universe; note chi = 0 and chi = pi are distinct antipodal points.

key_equations.name: Location of the point-like infinities
key_equations.meaning: Coordinates of spacelike and timelike infinities on the Einstein cylinder; scri+ is t' + r' = pi and scri- is t' - r' = -pi.

key_equations.name: Null infinities of Minkowski space
key_equations.latex: \mathcal I^+: t' + r' = \pi, \qquad \mathcal I^-: t' - r' = -\pi
key_equations.meaning: The two null edges of the Penrose triangle; outgoing rays (t' - r' = 2q fixed) end on scri+, incoming rays (t' + r' = 2p fixed) begin on scri-.
key_equations.symbols: Printed with unprimed t, r in Example 19.6; primes intended.

key_equations.name: Explicit Minkowski compactification (answer to Exercise 19.6)
key_equations.meaning: Closed-form map from Minkowski (t, r) to Penrose coordinates; not stated in the chapter text, given in Appendix E, and needed to draw Fig. 19.6.

key_equations.name: de Sitter (Universe 1), flat slicing
key_equations.meaning: Exponentially expanding flat slices; printed with 'ds' on the left where ds^2 is meant.

key_equations.name: de Sitter is conformal to a strip of the Einstein universe
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = \alpha^2 \sec^2 t'\; d\bar s^2_{\rm Einstein}, \quad -\tfrac{\pi}{2} < t' < \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \quad \alpha = 1/H
key_equations.meaning: de Sitter spacetime occupies a finite band of the Einstein cylinder, so its Penrose diagram is a square with spacelike scri+/-.
key_equations.symbols: d-bar-s^2 as in (19.19) with coordinates (t', chi, theta, phi); the book writes r in place of chi

key_equations.name: Robertson-Walker line element
key_equations.meaning: General homogeneous isotropic cosmology; Sigma given in a margin note.
key_equations.symbols: a(t) scale factor; k curvature index

key_equations.name: Conformal time
key_equations.meaning: Defines the time coordinate in which light rays move at 45 degrees and the scale factor becomes a conformal factor.

key_equations.name: Static conformal partner of Robertson-Walker
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = a^2\,d\bar s^2, \qquad d\bar s^2 = -d\tau^2 + d\chi^2 + \Sigma(\chi)^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)
key_equations.meaning: Any Robertson-Walker spacetime has the causal structure of a static metric; for k = 1 this is literally the Einstein universe.

key_equations.name: Image region for k = -1
key_equations.meaning: The open static metric maps to a diamond of half the Minkowski size; with tau > 0 only its upper half (t' > 0) is used for the open dust universe.

key_equations.name: k = -1 transformation (margin note 16, corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Maps -dtau^2 + dchi^2 + sinh^2 chi dOmega^2 to cosh(tau+chi) cosh(tau-chi) times the Einstein metric. The printed note has a plus sign in r' (making r' = t') and writes t for the conformal time tau.

key_equations.name: 1+1 Minkowski in light-cone coordinates
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = -du\,dv, \quad u = t - x,\ v = t + x
key_equations.meaning: Exercise 19.1 result; proper time and length follow from -du dv.

key_equations.name: Light-cone velocity
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate velocity of a uniformly moving particle in null coordinates: 1 at rest, 0 for a right-moving light ray, infinite for a left-moving one.

key_equations.name: de Sitter line element, Cartesian flat slicing
key_equations.latex: ds^2 = -d\hat t^2 + e^{2\hat t/\alpha}\left(d\hat x^2 + d\hat y^2 + d\hat z^2\right), \quad \alpha = H^{-1}
key_equations.meaning: Starting point of Exercise 19.4: the same Universe 1 metric as eqn 19.22 written in Cartesian comoving coordinates.

key_equations.name: de Sitter hyperboloid
key_equations.meaning: de Sitter spacetime as a surface in five-dimensional Minkowski space.

key_equations.name: Flat-slicing coordinates on the hyperboloid
key_equations.latex: \hat t = \alpha\ln\frac{w+v}{\alpha}, \quad \hat x = \frac{\alpha x}{w+v}, \quad \hat y = \frac{\alpha y}{w+v}, \quad \hat z = \frac{\alpha z}{w+v}
key_equations.meaning: Relates the flat-slicing coordinates of (19.32) to the embedding; only defined where w + v > 0, i.e. half the hyperboloid.

key_equations.name: Induced metric from 5D Minkowski space
key_equations.meaning: Exercise 19.4(a): the flat-slicing metric is the 5D Minkowski line element restricted to the hyperboloid (19.33).
key_equations.symbols: (v, w, x, y, z) embedding coordinates

key_equations.name: Global coordinates on the hyperboloid
key_equations.meaning: Coordinates covering the whole de Sitter hyperboloid with closed spatial slices.

key_equations.name: Global de Sitter line element (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Closed-slicing de Sitter: contracting then expanding 3-spheres. Printed with sin^2 phi where sin^2 chi is meant.

key_equations.name: de Sitter conformal time
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent to cosh(t/alpha) = sec t' and dt = alpha sec t' dt', which turns (19.37) into (19.23).

key_equations.name: Redshift from conformal invariance (Exercise 19.5)
key_equations.meaning: A wave e^{iB tau} in the static conformal metric has instantaneous frequency B/a in cosmic time.

key_equations.name: Friedmann equation for closed dust, rearranged
key_equations.meaning: From adot^2 + 1 = C/a for k = 1, Lambda = 0.
key_equations.symbols: C constant set by the dust density (C = 8 pi a0^3 rho_d / 3 in GA ch18)

key_equations.name: Scale factor versus conformal time, implicit
key_equations.meaning: Solution of the closed dust model in terms of conformal time eta.
key_equations.symbols: eta conformal time (dt = a d eta)

key_equations.name: Cycloid solution of Universe 6
key_equations.meaning: Universe lasts 0 < eta < 2 pi: maximum a = C at eta = pi, Crunch at cosmic time pi C. Light covers comoving angle eta, so a ray circles the 3-sphere exactly once in the lifetime.

figures.label: Fig. 19.1(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A single Minkowski light cone whose two nappes mark the future and the past.
figures.visual_description: A double cone drawn in perspective with its vertex at the origin of t (vertical), x (horizontal) and y (oblique) axes. The upper nappe contains the word FUTURE near its elliptical rim and the lower nappe, lightly hatched at its rim, contains PAST.
figures.what_it_teaches: Locally the light cone splits directions unambiguously into future-pointing and past-pointing.

redesign.idea: Rotatable 3D light cone with a draggable 4-vector that changes colour (future timelike, past timelike, null, spacelike) as it crosses the cone.
redesign.interaction: Drag the vector tip; the classification label and the sign of g(v,v) update live.

figures.label: Fig. 19.1(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A time-orientable spacetime strip whose left and right edges are glued into a cylinder; all cones agree on which way is future.
figures.visual_description: A rectangular strip bounded on left and right by dotted vertical lines, filled with a 3-by-5 array of small upright hourglass shapes (double light cones), all identical in orientation. A curved double-headed arrow beneath the strip joins the two dotted edges and is labelled 'identify'.
figures.what_it_teaches: After gluing, a continuous future direction exists everywhere, so the spacetime is time-orientable.

redesign.idea: Combine (b) and (c) into a single strip of light cones that the learner can glue into a cylinder or a Mobius-type band, with the future nappe tinted.
redesign.interaction: Slider sets how much the cones rotate across the strip (0 or 180 degrees); a 'glue' button animates wrapping; a walker carrying a future arrow goes once around and a warning flashes if it comes back pointing into the past.

figures.label: Fig. 19.1(c)
figures.caption_paraphrase: A non-orientable strip in which no consistent future direction survives the gluing.
figures.visual_description: The same dotted-edge strip and 'identify' arrow as panel (b), but in each row the hourglass cones rotate progressively from left to right: upright at the left edge, tilted, lying sideways like a bow tie in the middle, tilted the other way, and upright again at the right edge, so that across the strip each cone has turned through half a revolution before the edges are joined.
figures.what_it_teaches: Local cones can all be perfectly good while global gluing swaps future and past, so time orientability is a global property.

redesign.idea: Covered by the combined (b)/(c) interactive strip.
redesign.interaction: Same component as Fig. 19.1(b), preset to the twisted configuration.

figures.label: Fig. 19.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: A closed timelike curve.
figures.visual_description: A horizontal ellipse drawn as a closed loop, with about eight light cones sitting on it, each drawn as a fan of ruled lines (double cone). The cones tilt progressively around the loop so that the direction along the ellipse always lies inside each cone; at the front and back of the loop the cones look like upright bow ties, at the sides they are seen end-on.
figures.what_it_teaches: If light cones tip over enough around a loop, a world line can stay timelike everywhere yet close on itself, allowing an observer to meet their own past.

redesign.idea: A ring of light cones whose tilt is controlled by a slider; a particle traces the ring only if the tangent stays inside every cone.
redesign.interaction: Increase the tilt; when the loop becomes timelike the particle can complete the circuit and a 'meets its own past' event is highlighted, otherwise it is forced upward into a helix.

figures.label: Fig. 19.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: The hyperbolic plane shown conformally as a disc.
figures.visual_description: A circular Poincare disc tiled with alternating black and white triangles whose sides are circular arcs. Triangles near the centre are large; they shrink rapidly and multiply toward the boundary circle, which appears as a dense grey rim.
figures.what_it_teaches: An infinite space can be drawn inside a finite boundary while keeping angles correct; apparent size is not true size, exactly the trade-off made by Penrose diagrams.

redesign.idea: Interactive Poincare disc in which a triangle of fixed hyperbolic size can be dragged toward the rim, with its angle sum and true area displayed.
redesign.interaction: Drag a hyperbolic triangle; its drawn size shrinks near the edge while its angles and area readouts stay fixed; toggle an overlay of a Penrose triangle to draw the analogy.

figures.label: Fig. 19.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Minkowski space on a t-r plane: horizontal lines spacelike, vertical lines timelike, dotted diagonals null.
figures.visual_description: A square grid with a vertical t axis and horizontal r axis meeting at the left, where the grid starts. Two dotted straight lines leave the origin at 45 degrees, one rising to the upper right and one descending to the lower right, forming half of a light cone.
figures.what_it_teaches: The starting picture before compactification: straight constant-r and constant-t lines and 45-degree null rays on an infinite half-plane.

redesign.idea: First frame of a morphing animation from the t-r grid to the Penrose triangle.
redesign.interaction: Scrub a slider from 0 to 1 blending (t, r) into (t', r') coordinates; grid lines bend into Penrose curves while 45-degree rays stay straight.

figures.label: Fig. 19.5(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Arrows indicating the five different kinds of infinity in Minkowski space.
figures.visual_description: Axes t (up) and r (right). Clusters of three parallel arrows point: straight up toward a label i+, straight down toward i-, rightward along the r axis toward i0, diagonally up-right toward a script I+ label, and diagonally down-right toward a script I- label.
figures.what_it_teaches: Infinity is not one place: timelike, spacelike and null curves run off to different kinds of infinity.

redesign.idea: Launch curves from the origin on an infinite t-r plot and watch where each type heads, then snap the arrows onto the edges of the Penrose triangle.
redesign.interaction: Pick timelike, null or spacelike, set a velocity; the curve runs off-screen and a labelled marker lights up on the matching infinity of an adjacent Penrose triangle.

figures.label: Fig. 19.5(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The Minkowski Penrose diagram: all of Minkowski space fills the shaded triangle.
figures.visual_description: A grey right triangle with its vertical edge on the t' axis from i- (bottom) to i+ (top); two 45-degree edges, labelled scri+ above and scri- below, meet at the rightmost vertex i0 on the r' axis.
figures.what_it_teaches: The whole infinite spacetime fits in a finite region whose edges and corners are the infinities.

redesign.idea: Base Penrose-diagram component reused through the course: hovering any boundary piece names it and shows which curves end there.
redesign.interaction: Hover or tap boundary segments and vertices; a tooltip explains the infinity and a sample curve ending there is drawn.

figures.label: Fig. 19.6(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Constant-r (timelike) surfaces of Minkowski space on the Penrose diagram.
figures.visual_description: The Penrose triangle (i+ top, i- bottom, i0 right, scri+ and scri- edges) containing five curves that each start at i- and end at i+, bowing to the right; the larger the Minkowski radius, the further the curve bulges toward i0.
figures.what_it_teaches: Every static observer's world line, and by extension every massive particle, begins at i- and ends at i+.

redesign.idea: Penrose triangle with a slider for the Minkowski radius r of a static observer and a second slider for the speed beta of a moving one.
redesign.interaction: Move r: the constant-r curve slides between the axis and the scri edges; move beta: a straight-line world line through the origin maps to a curve still ending at i+.

figures.label: Fig. 19.6(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Constant-t (spacelike) surfaces of Minkowski space on the Penrose diagram.
figures.visual_description: The same triangle with about ten curves that leave the vertical axis at different heights and all converge on the i0 vertex; those above the r' axis sag downward toward i0, those below rise toward it, and the t = 0 slice is the straight horizontal axis.
figures.what_it_teaches: All spatial slices, and all spacelike geodesics, run out to the single point i0.

redesign.idea: Same component as Fig. 19.6(a) with a time slider that sweeps a constant-t slice through the triangle.
redesign.interaction: Drag t from minus to plus large values; the slice curve moves from near scri- through the axis to near scri+, always pinned at i0.

figures.label: Fig. 19.7(a)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Constant-r and constant-t curves together criss-cross the Minkowski Penrose diagram.
figures.visual_description: The Penrose triangle overlaid with both families of curves from Fig. 19.6: curves bunched toward i+ and i- from the timelike family and curves fanning into i0 from the spacelike family, forming a distorted curvilinear grid that is densest near the boundary.
figures.what_it_teaches: The ordinary rectangular Minkowski grid becomes a curved mesh; the compression near the edges shows distances are not preserved.

redesign.idea: Grid-morph animation paired with Fig. 19.4: the rectangular grid continuously deforms into this mesh.
redesign.interaction: Toggle each family on and off and adjust grid spacing; hover a cell to see its true Minkowski area versus drawn area.

figures.label: Fig. 19.7(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Null surfaces stay straight 45-degree lines running from scri- to scri+. (The inventory label 'Fig. 19.6' attached to this image is wrong.)
figures.visual_description: The empty Penrose triangle with two reflected light rays. Each starts on the scri- edge below the r' axis and runs up and to the left, parallel to scri+, until it meets the vertical axis above the r' axis; from that point a shorter segment runs up and to the right, parallel to scri-, to end on scri+. The two paths make sideways V shapes opening to the right, and they cross each other once.
figures.what_it_teaches: The map is built so that radial light rays remain at 45 degrees; an incoming ray passes through r' = 0 and leaves as an outgoing ray, so every ray starts on scri- and ends on scri+.
concepts: conformal invariance of the light-cone structure

redesign.idea: Light-pulse emitter on the Penrose triangle.
redesign.interaction: Click any point to emit a spherical flash; the outgoing and incoming rays are drawn at 45 degrees, the incoming one bouncing through the axis, and both end highlighted on scri+.

figures.label: Fig. 19.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: The past light cone of an event P on the Minkowski Penrose diagram.
figures.visual_description: The Penrose triangle with a point P just above the r' axis. Two 45-degree lines descend from P, one to the left meeting the vertical axis and one to the right meeting the scri- edge. The region below P bounded by these lines, the axis down to i-, and scri- is shaded grey.
figures.what_it_teaches: The observer at P knows only about the shaded causal past; because it always contains i-, waiting long enough brings every particle's history into view.

redesign.idea: Draggable observer event with shaded causal past, shared across Minkowski, de Sitter and Robertson-Walker diagrams.
redesign.interaction: Drag P upward along a world line; the shaded past grows; comoving world lines turn from grey to coloured once they enter it, directly comparing the no-horizon and horizon cases.

figures.label: Fig. 19.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: Minkowski space in light-cone coordinates; each point is a sphere of radius r.
figures.visual_description: A half-plane diagram: vertical t axis (extending both above and below the horizontal r axis) with r running to the right from it. Two families of parallel straight lines at plus and minus 45 degrees fill the region r >= 0; the up-right family is tagged 'u = const.' near the top and the down-right family 'v = const.' near the bottom.
figures.what_it_teaches: Null coordinates label radial light rays directly: outgoing rays are constant u, incoming rays constant v.

redesign.idea: Toggle between (t, r) and (u, v) readouts on the same plane.
redesign.interaction: Hover a point to read t, r, u, v; click to highlight the constant-u and constant-v lines through it and the 2-sphere it represents.

figures.label: Fig. 19.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: The inverse-tangent function squeezes the infinite x axis into a finite angular range.
figures.visual_description: Graph of y = arctan x on horizontal x and vertical axes: an S-shaped curve through the origin levelling off toward y = pi/2 on the right and y = -pi/2 on the left, with dotted horizontal arrows pointing from the far ends toward the pi/2 and -pi/2 marks.
figures.what_it_teaches: The single trick behind compactification: a monotone function with finite limits brings infinity to a finite coordinate value.

redesign.idea: Number line squeezed onto a finite segment.
redesign.interaction: Drag a bead along an infinite x axis (auto-scaling); its image on the y segment approaches pi/2 ever more slowly; compare arctan with tanh and 2/pi arctan.

figures.label: Fig. 19.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: The Einstein static universe drawn as a cylinder; each horizontal circle stands for a 3-sphere.
figures.visual_description: A vertical cylinder with three horizontal circles (bottom, middle, top). A solid vertical line on the front face is marked chi = 0 at its foot; a dotted vertical line on the back is marked chi = pi at its top. A long double-headed arrow on the right is labelled t = infinity at the top, t = 0 at the middle and t = minus infinity at the bottom. Two curved arrows at the base, both labelled chi, point away from the front line in opposite directions around the cylinder.
figures.what_it_teaches: The Einstein universe has cylindrical topology (time times a closed space); chi runs from 0 to pi both ways round, since each circle is a slice through a 3-sphere.

redesign.idea: 3D Einstein cylinder that serves as the canvas for every patch in the chapter.
redesign.interaction: Orbit the cylinder; hover to read (t', chi); a toggle shows that the front meridian is chi = 0 and the back meridian chi = pi, with chi increasing both ways round.

figures.label: Fig. 19.12
figures.caption_paraphrase: Minkowski space mapped to a bounded patch of the larger Einstein static universe.
figures.visual_description: A cylinder with circles labelled t' = pi (upper), t' = 0 (middle) and t' = -pi (lower). A hatched region wraps around the cylinder between i- on the front of the lower circle and i+ on the front of the upper circle, with i0 at the back on the t' = 0 circle; its curved upper and lower edges are labelled scri+ and scri-. Dashed vertical lines mark r' = 0 at the front and r' = pi at the back; a small up-arrow at the left indicates the time direction.
figures.what_it_teaches: Minkowski space is a finite piece of the Einstein cylinder; its edges within the cylinder are its conformal infinity, and flattening one half of the patch gives the Penrose triangle.

redesign.idea: Animated wrapping of the Penrose triangle (reflected to a diamond) onto the Einstein cylinder.
redesign.interaction: Slider unwraps the patch from the cylinder into the flat (t', r') plane; hovering i+, i0, i-, scri+/- highlights the same point on both views.

figures.label: Fig. 19.13
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram of de Sitter spacetime.
figures.visual_description: A square grid with vertical t' axis from -pi/2 to pi/2 (0 marked midway) and horizontal chi axis from 0 to pi. The top edge is labelled scri+ and the bottom edge scri-.
figures.what_it_teaches: de Sitter has no point-like i+, i- or i0: its future and past infinities are whole horizontal (spacelike) edges.

redesign.idea: Side-by-side Minkowski triangle and de Sitter square with a shared observer and light-cone tool.
redesign.interaction: Drag an observer event in each; compare how much of the lower boundary its past cone reaches; overlay the half covered by flat-slicing coordinates.

figures.label: Fig. 19.14
figures.caption_paraphrase: Particle horizon at P in a spacetime with spacelike past null infinity: some world lines have not yet entered P's past light cone.
figures.visual_description: A thick curved line at the bottom labelled scri- from which many wavy world lines rise. One bold line, labelled 'Observer's world line', carries the event P, from which two straight lines descend to scri- and are labelled 'Past null cone of P'. World lines that cross inside this cone are bracketed at the top as observed at P; the world lines farther out on both the left and right are drawn hatched, and a bracket on the right marks them as not observed at P, with 'World lines' written along the right-hand bundle.
figures.what_it_teaches: When the past boundary is spacelike, a past light cone catches only a finite set of world lines; the boundary between caught and uncaught particles is the particle horizon.

redesign.idea: Animated observer climbing a world line in de Sitter or Einstein-de Sitter conformal coordinates.
redesign.interaction: Play or scrub observer time; the past cone widens and world lines light up as they cross in, with a counter of visible galaxies and the horizon's comoving radius.

figures.label: Fig. 19.15
figures.caption_paraphrase: In de Sitter space, the observer at chi = 0 reaching t' = pi/2 has a past light cone that reaches every chi only at the bottom edge.
figures.visual_description: The de Sitter square grid (t' from -pi/2 to pi/2, chi from 0 to pi, scri+ on top, scri- on bottom) with the lower-left triangle below the diagonal from the top-left corner (chi = 0, t' = pi/2) to the bottom-right corner (chi = pi, t' = -pi/2) shaded grey.
figures.what_it_teaches: The shaded triangle is everything the chi = 0 observer will ever see; the diagonal is the future event horizon, and the unshaded upper-right triangle can never be seen, even though every comoving world line is eventually glimpsed near scri-.

redesign.idea: de Sitter square with an observer at chi = 0 whose past cone is animated up to scri+.
redesign.interaction: Scrub the observer's conformal time; shaded region grows until it freezes at the event horizon; a second slider places a galaxy at chi and marks the last event on it that will ever be seen.

figures.label: Fig. 19.16
figures.caption_paraphrase: Future event horizon of an observer on world line O; hatched events beyond it are never seen by O.
figures.visual_description: A horizontal band between a wavy upper curve labelled scri+ and a wavy lower curve labelled scri-. Two world lines, Q (left) and O (right), rise from the lower boundary. A point P on O sends two straight lines down to scri-, its past cone. From O's endpoint on scri+ a larger inverted V of straight lines descends to scri-, labelled O's future event horizon; Q crosses its left arm at a point R. Everything outside this large inverted V, on both the left and right sides of the band over its full height, is hatched.
figures.what_it_teaches: Another particle's history is visible only up to R, where it crosses O's event horizon; R itself arrives in O's sky only in the infinite future.

redesign.idea: Two-observer de Sitter simulation: O watches a clock carried by Q.
redesign.interaction: Advance O's time; a panel shows Q's clock reading as received by O, which approaches but never passes the reading at R, with growing redshift.

figures.label: Fig. 19.17
figures.caption_paraphrase: Past and future event horizons of a world line W divide spacetime into regions.
figures.visual_description: A wide rectangle (about twice as wide as tall) with a dashed vertical world line W in the centre carrying an upward arrow. Two straight lines run from the top-centre point down to the bottom corners and two from the bottom-centre point up to the top corners, forming a central diamond marked I. The two top triangles (light grey) are marked II, the two bottom triangles (darker grey) are marked III; the left and right side triangles are white and unlabelled.
figures.what_it_teaches: Relative to a world line: I can be seen and influenced, II influenced but never seen, III seen but never influenced; the unlabelled side regions are causally cut off both ways.
concepts: causal regions of a world line

redesign.idea: Colour-coded causal-region map for an arbitrary world line in de Sitter space.
redesign.interaction: Drag the world line's endpoints on scri- and scri+ (or tilt it); the four regions recolour live and a click on any event reports 'can see / can influence'.

figures.label: Fig. 19.18
figures.caption_paraphrase: Causal structure of the Robertson-Walker spacetimes as patches on Einstein cylinders.
figures.visual_description: Three identical cylinders labelled k = 1, k = 0 and k = -1, with dashed circles marked t' = pi (upper) and t' = 0 (lower) by arrows on the right. For k = 1 the entire band between the two circles is hatched. For k = 0 a hatched region rises from the t' = 0 circle to a peak touching t' = pi at the front and slopes down around the sides. For k = -1 a much lower hatched peak rises only about half way toward t' = pi. Dashed lines beneath the k = 0 cylinder mark chi = 0 and chi = pi with small chi arrows, and beneath the k = -1 cylinder mark chi = 0 and chi = pi/2, the widest extent of the open patch.
figures.what_it_teaches: Each curvature case occupies a different region of the same Einstein canvas, bounded below by the Big Bang at t' = 0; only k = 1 fills a full band and is also bounded above.

redesign.idea: Einstein cylinder with a k selector and matter-content selector that paints the corresponding patch.
redesign.interaction: Choose k and equation of state (dust, radiation, Lambda); the patch shape and its flattened Penrose diagram update, showing that closed dust needs a band of height 2 pi in chi-units.

figures.label: Fig. 19.19
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram for the flat and open Robertson-Walker spacetimes, with the spacelike Big-Bang singularity as a double line.
figures.visual_description: A right triangle on t' (vertical) and chi (horizontal) axes: the vertical edge rises from 0 to i+, a diagonal edge labelled scri+ descends to i0 on the chi axis, and the bottom edge is drawn as a double line labelled scri-(t' = 0).
figures.what_it_teaches: Flat and open Big-Bang universes look like the upper half of Minkowski space sitting on a spacelike singularity: no future event horizon, but a particle horizon.

redesign.idea: Einstein-de Sitter observer on this triangle with a live particle-horizon readout in physical units.
redesign.interaction: Drag the observer's cosmic time; past cone reaches the double line at a comoving radius that grows; readout shows the proper horizon distance 3ct.

figures.label: Fig. 19.20
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose diagram for the closed Robertson-Walker spacetime with Big-Bang and Big-Crunch singularities as double lines.
figures.visual_description: A square on t' (0 to pi) and chi (0 to pi) axes, with its bottom edge a double line labelled scri-(t' = 0) and its top edge a double line labelled scri+(t' = pi); the vertical sides are plain lines.
figures.what_it_teaches: A closed recollapsing universe is bounded by spacelike singularities in both past and future, so it has both particle and event horizons.

redesign.idea: Accurate closed-dust Penrose diagram (width pi, height 2 pi in conformal time) with a toggle to the book's rescaled square.
redesign.interaction: Toggle 'true 3-sphere coordinates' versus 'great-circle picture'; light rays reflect through the poles in the first and wrap around in the second, arriving at the same events.

figures.label: Fig. 19.21(a)
