figures.caption_paraphrase: For the closed Universe 6, an observer sitting at chi = 0 has received light from every grid position by conformal time pi/2, because the left and right edges of the diagram are identified.
figures.visual_description: The closed-universe square grid (double lines at t' = 0 and t' = pi) with several short arrows at 45 degrees in the lower half: arrows from the bottom-middle region point up-left toward the left edge and others point up-right toward the right edge, converging on the edges near t' = pi/2.
figures.what_it_teaches: With the chi direction treated as periodic, the observer's past cone reaches both ways round the universe and has covered all of space by maximum expansion.

redesign.idea: Periodic-strip Penrose diagram for a closed universe, drawable as a flat strip or rolled into a cylinder.
redesign.interaction: Scrub observer time; past cone wraps across the identified edges; sources change from unseen to seen once to seen twice, with counts.

figures.label: Fig. 19.21(b)
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two images of one star reaching the observer in the closed universe. (The inventory label 'Fig. 19.22' on this image is wrong.)
figures.visual_description: The same 6-by-6 square grid. A long straight line starts on the bottom edge at about chi = 5 pi/6 and rises up and to the left to an arrowhead on the left edge (chi = 0) at about t' = 5 pi/6. A short arrow starts at the same chi at about t' = 2 pi/3 and rises up and to the right to the right edge (chi = pi) at the same height t' = 5 pi/6. Since the two edges are identified, one source is seen twice at once: via the long route with light that left it at the Big Bang, and via the short route with light that left it much later.
figures.what_it_teaches: Once the past cone has wrapped around, a source is seen both by the short route and the long route, the two images having left it at different epochs.

redesign.idea: Same periodic-strip component with a selectable source world line.
redesign.interaction: Click a source; both received light paths are drawn with emission epochs and redshift or blueshift of each image.

figures.label: Fig. 19.22
figures.caption_paraphrase: Light paths round a closed universe drawn as a circle: (a) at maximum expansion light from all stars arrives, half from each side; (b) during contraction star B is seen along both the short and long routes.
figures.visual_description: Two panels, each a pair of concentric circles (a ring) with black dots for stars on it and a point A at the right. In (a) a solid arrowed arc runs clockwise over the top from the leftmost point to A and a dashed arc runs anticlockwise under the bottom to A. In (b) a star B sits at lower right near A; a short arrowed arc goes from B up to A and a dashed arc goes the long way round to A.
figures.what_it_teaches: Space in the closed model is a loop, so light can arrive from both directions; the angle round the drawn circle is twice the book's chi coordinate.

redesign.idea: Breathing ring universe synchronised with the Penrose strip: the ring radius follows the cycloid a(eta).
redesign.interaction: Play the universe's life; photons crawl round the ring at fixed conformal speed; an observer's sky shows images appearing, duplicating and shifting colour from red to blue.

worked_examples.label: Example 19.1
worked_examples.problem: Illustrate a conformal representation using a geometry the reader has met: the hyperbolic plane.
worked_examples.method: Recalls that triangle angles sum to less than pi in Lobachevskian geometry and presents the Escher-style triangle tiling of the Poincare disc, pointing out that geodesics meet the rim at right angles and that all triangles are congruent despite their drawn sizes.
worked_examples.key_insight: A conformal picture keeps angles and lets sizes shrink, which is how an infinite space can be drawn inside a finite boundary.

worked_examples.label: Example 19.2
worked_examples.problem: What can an observer at event P in Minkowski space know about, and is any particle permanently hidden?
worked_examples.method: Shades the region bounded by P's backward 45-degree rays on the Penrose triangle, notes that timelike geodesics end at i+ and that P's causal past always includes i-.
worked_examples.key_insight: Since every world line starts at the point i-, every particle is eventually seen: Minkowski space has no particle horizon, and at i+ there is no event horizon either.
worked_examples.result: An inertial Minkowski observer can in principle see every particle in the universe.

worked_examples.label: Example 19.3
worked_examples.problem: Rewrite the Minkowski line element in coordinates adapted to light rays.
worked_examples.method: Convert to spherical polars, define u = t - r and v = t + r, substitute dt and dr, and note r = (v - u)/2 in the angular term.
worked_examples.key_insight: Radial null rays become coordinate lines, and suppressing the 2-sphere lets the whole spacetime be drawn in 2D with each point meaning a sphere.

worked_examples.label: Example 19.4
worked_examples.problem: Can we reach v = infinity simply by the substitution V = 1/v?
worked_examples.method: Substitute, find a 1/V^2 factor and a (1/V - u)^2 factor that blow up at V = 0; then multiply by V^2, defining an unphysical metric g-bar with eta = g-bar / V^2, which is regular at V = 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Coordinates alone cannot tame infinity; a conformal factor vanishing there can, and because it preserves light cones the regular metric tells the truth about causal structure.
worked_examples.result: d-bar-s^2 = du dV + (1/4)(1 - uV)^2 dOmega^2 (eqn 19.10) and the two-step compactification strategy.

worked_examples.label: Example 19.5
worked_examples.problem: Compactify all of Minkowski space and identify the resulting conformal metric.
worked_examples.method: Choose Omega^2 = 4/[(1+u^2)(1+v^2)], substitute u = tan q, v = tan p, use sec^2 = 1 + tan^2 and tan p - tan q = sin(p-q)/(cos p cos q), strip off 1/Omega^2, then set t' = p + q, r' = p - q.
worked_examples.key_insight: The rescaled metric is precisely the Einstein static universe, so Minkowski space is a bounded triangle-shaped patch of a known spacetime whose edge is Minkowski's infinity.
worked_examples.result: d-bar-s^2 = -dt'^2 + dr'^2 + sin^2 r' dOmega^2 on -pi < t' +/- r' < pi, r' >= 0 (eqns 19.15-19.18).

worked_examples.label: Example 19.6
worked_examples.problem: Locate the infinities of Minkowski space in the compactified coordinates.
worked_examples.method: Read off the patch corners on the Einstein cylinder and the null lines joining them, using t' - r' = 2q and t' + r' = 2p constant along outgoing and incoming rays.
worked_examples.key_insight: Outgoing rays all end on the null line t' + r' = pi and incoming rays all begin on t' - r' = -pi; the timelike and spacelike infinities are single points.
worked_examples.result: i0 = (0, pi), i+ = (pi, 0), i- = (-pi, 0); scri+: t' + r' = pi; scri-: t' - r' = -pi.

worked_examples.label: Example 19.7
worked_examples.problem: In a spacetime with event horizons, what does observer O see of another particle Q?
worked_examples.method: On Fig. 19.16, note that part of Q lies in P's past cone (inside the particle horizon), draw O's future event horizon from O's endpoint on scri+, and find its crossing R with Q.
worked_examples.key_insight: Events on Q later than R are invisible to O forever, and R itself enters O's past cone only at O's infinite future.
worked_examples.result: O sees Q's history only up to R, with R appearing at infinity.

worked_examples.label: Example 19.8
worked_examples.problem: Classify spacetime regions relative to a world line W using its past and future event horizons.
worked_examples.method: Draw the past cone of W's end on future infinity and the future cone of W's start on past infinity; label the regions they cut out.
worked_examples.key_insight: Seeing and influencing are separate questions with separate horizons.
worked_examples.result: Region I: seen and influenced; II: influenced, never seen; III: seen, never influenced (side regions: neither, unlabelled).
concepts: causal regions of a world line

worked_examples.label: Example 19.9
worked_examples.problem: Show that pressure-free, Lambda = 0 Robertson-Walker spacetimes are conformal to regions of the Einstein static universe.
worked_examples.method: Use conformal time to factor out a^2. For k = 1 set chi = r', tau = t' directly; for k = 0 reuse the Minkowski compactification restricted to tau > 0; for k = -1 apply the tanh-arctan transformation of margin note 16.
worked_examples.key_insight: The Big Bang at tau = 0 becomes the t' = 0 slice, so every model's patch sits on a spacelike lower boundary; the curvature index decides the patch shape.
worked_examples.result: k = 1: band starting at t' = 0 (the book says ending at t' = pi; for dust the conformal lifetime is actually 2 pi); k = 0: upper half of the Minkowski triangle; k = -1: region -pi/2 <= t' +/- r' <= pi/2 with t' > 0.

worked_examples.label: Example 19.10
worked_examples.problem: Describe what an observer sees over the life of the closed dust Universe 6.
worked_examples.method: Follow the observer's past light cone on the k = 1 diagram with the chi direction treated as periodic, supplemented by a ring picture of space; then compare scale factors at emission and reception for the shifts.
worked_examples.key_insight: The past cone keeps growing through recollapse, so sources are first seen once, all at maximum expansion, then twice; light from one's own early position would complete the loop exactly at the Crunch.
worked_examples.result: Increasing numbers of stars during expansion; every star (half from each side) at maximum expansion; duplicate images during contraction; redshifts early, mixed red and blue during collapse, mostly blue at the end.

worked_examples.problem: Where do the coordinate lines and light rays of Minkowski space go on the Penrose diagram?
worked_examples.method: Qualitative mapping argument supported by Figs 19.6-19.7: constant-r lines, constant-t lines and 45-degree rays, with the r' = 0 axis acting as a mirror for incoming rays.
worked_examples.key_insight: The endpoints of curves are dictated by their causal type, which is exactly what the diagram is designed to show.
worked_examples.result: Timelike: i- to i+; spacelike: i0 to i0 through the origin; null: scri- to scri+.

worked_examples.problem: Show de Sitter spacetime is conformal to part of the Einstein static universe (text claim, derivation in Exercise 19.4).
worked_examples.method: Embed de Sitter as a hyperboloid, introduce global cosh coordinates, then define t' by tan(t'/2 + pi/4) = e^{t/alpha}, which gives cosh(t/alpha) = sec t' and dt = alpha sec t' dt'.
worked_examples.key_insight: The conformal factor alpha^2 sec^2 t' blows up at t' = +/- pi/2, so infinite cosmic time fits into a strip of height pi.
worked_examples.result: ds^2 = alpha^2 sec^2 t' [ -dt'^2 + dchi^2 + sin^2 chi dOmega^2 ].

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The everyday horizon separates what can be seen from what cannot; spacetime horizons do the same for events an observer can access.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A skyline horizon moves as you walk and hides objects behind curvature of a surface; cosmological horizons are defined over an observer's entire history and some (event horizons) never recede.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split screen: a walker on a globe watching ships vanish, alongside a de Sitter observer watching galaxies freeze at the event horizon.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A familiar image in which infinitely many equal triangles fit inside a circle, sizes shrinking but angles intact, primes the idea of drawing infinity at a finite edge.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: It is a Riemannian (positive-definite) space with no light cones; Penrose diagrams preserve null directions rather than all Euclidean angles on the page.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Morph from the Poincare disc to the Penrose triangle, highlighting that both push infinity to a boundary.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The graph of arctan shows at a glance how the entire infinite axis is packed into a finite interval.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The choice of squashing function is not unique, and only special choices yield a nice conformal factor.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Bead-on-a-line demo comparing arctan and tanh squashing.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Frames the diagram as a deliberately distorted sketch that keeps only what matters for causality.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Learners may over-read cartoons, e.g. taking lengths or curve shapes literally.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Wrapping a sheet of cones into a cylinder, with or without a twist
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gluing the edges of a strip of light cones shows how a global inconsistency can arise from locally fine cones.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The picture is two-dimensional and the gluing is imposed by hand; real non-orientable spacetimes are exotic.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Entropy increase as the arrow of time
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Suggested as a practical way to decide which half of the cones to call future.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Thermodynamic arrow is a physical heuristic, not part of the geometric definition; orientability can hold or fail independently.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Einstein static cylinder as a common canvas
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Every spacetime in the chapter is painted as a patch on the same cylinder, so their causal shapes can be compared directly.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The cylinder hides two dimensions and each circle is really a 3-sphere; chi runs 0 to pi both ways round, which confuses readers.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Gallery of patches on one rotatable cylinder with a spacetime selector.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Seeing the back of your own head
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Dramatises that light could travel all the way around a closed universe, and then shows the timing makes it coincide with the Crunch.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Assumes a transparent universe and ignores that the source images would be infinitely blueshifted and the observer destroyed.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Ring-universe animation where the observer's own early light approaches from behind as the ring shrinks to zero.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Illustrates why closed timelike loops would produce contradictions.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Consistency-condition resolutions exist; the paradox motivates but does not prove impossibility.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Pointing arrows toward infinity ('To infinity, and beyond!')
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: A playful reference to a film catchphrase opens the question of where infinity actually is, followed by literal arrows in Fig. 19.5(a).
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Arrows convey direction but not the point-versus-surface nature of each infinity; the authors admit this is not a grown-up treatment.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Infinity is a single place at the edge of spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Minkowski space has five distinct infinities: two timelike points, one spacelike point and two null surfaces, distinguished by which kind of curve reaches them.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In ordinary calculus there is just 'plus or minus infinity'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A Penrose diagram shows distances, durations or the actual shape of world lines faithfully.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only the conformal structure is kept: angles in the sense of null directions and causal relations. Straight Minkowski grid lines become curves, and equal intervals look tiny near the boundary.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It looks like an ordinary spacetime diagram with 45-degree light rays.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The unphysical conformal metric is just Minkowski in new clothes, still flat.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The rescaled metric is the Einstein static universe, which is curved; conformal rescaling preserves light cones but changes curvature, lengths and even which timelike curves are geodesics.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It was obtained from Minkowski space and shares its light cones.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Given enough time, any observer can receive signals from the whole universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: True in Minkowski space, but in de Sitter and closed universes future event horizons hide some events forever, and particle horizons hide some world lines at any finite time.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Light travels forever and the universe seems to be waiting to be seen.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Particle horizons and event horizons are the same thing.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A particle horizon concerns which world lines have been seen by a given moment and grows; an event horizon concerns which events will ever be seen and is fixed by the observer's endpoint at future infinity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both are boundaries of what is visible and both are called horizons.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Horizons are fixed physical surfaces in space.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Cosmological horizons depend on which observer and, for particle horizons, on when; each observer carries their own.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The black-hole horizon is often pictured as a physical membrane.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: In de Sitter space, an observer located half-way across (chi = pi/2) could have seen the whole chi range earlier than the observer at chi = 0.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: All positions are equivalent by homogeneity; chi is radius-like, so the relevant question is how far a ray travels outward from the observer, which is the same for everyone.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: On the square diagram a point in the middle seems to have past cones reaching both edges sooner.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Big Bang was a point, an explosion at a particular place.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the conformal picture the Big Bang is a spacelike surface from which every world line emerges, at every location at once.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Popular imagery and the word 'bang' suggest a centre.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Singularities and infinities are the same kind of thing because both sit on the edge of the diagram.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Both are boundaries, but a singularity can be a finite proper time away and signals the breakdown of physics; an infinity is by definition infinitely far.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Both are drawn as edges of the Penrose diagram.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: In a closed universe a traveller or signal could circle the universe and return to its start.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the closed dust model even light only just completes one circuit at the moment of the Crunch; no massive particle can go round.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: A finite closed space suggests finite travel times.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The chi coordinate is the angle around the circle in the ring picture of the closed universe.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In the book's ring picture the angle round the circle is twice chi; in true 3-sphere coordinates chi = 0 and chi = pi are antipodal points, not the same point.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The text identifies chi = 0 with chi = pi on the diagram.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Every spacetime automatically has a well-defined future direction.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Time orientability is a global condition that can fail even when every local light cone is ordinary.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Locally there is always a future cone.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Big-Bang edge labelled scri- in Figs 19.19-19.21 is past null infinity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It is a spacelike singularity at finite past proper time; the label is borrowed loosely. Past null infinity of Minkowski or de Sitter is infinitely far away.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The same symbol is used for both.

thought_experiments.name: Waiting forever for news from everywhere
thought_experiments.setup: An observer stays put and asks whether, given unlimited time, light from every event or every particle will eventually arrive.
thought_experiments.lesson: The answer depends on the global causal structure: yes for Minkowski space, no for de Sitter (event horizon), and only eventually for particles in Big-Bang models.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Same observer tool dropped into three Penrose diagrams with a 'fraction of universe seen' meter.

thought_experiments.name: Travelling round a timelike loop
thought_experiments.setup: A particle follows a closed timelike curve through tilted light cones and meets its own earlier self.
thought_experiments.lesson: Closed timelike curves are the unique loophole in local causality and bring paradoxes, which is why ordinary spacetimes are assumed free of them.

thought_experiments.name: Watching a distant particle freeze at the de Sitter horizon
thought_experiments.setup: Observer O in de Sitter space watches particle Q, whose world line crosses O's future event horizon at R.
thought_experiments.lesson: O sees Q's history only up to R, and R appears only at O's infinite future: the cosmological version of an object freezing at a black-hole horizon.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Received-clock display for Q that asymptotes to the reading at R.

thought_experiments.name: Stargazing through the life of a closed universe
thought_experiments.setup: An observer in Universe 6, with a star at every position, records the sky from Big Bang to Big Crunch.
thought_experiments.lesson: More stars appear during expansion, all are visible at maximum expansion from both directions, duplicates appear during collapse, and one's own earliest light would arrive only at the Crunch; red- turns to blueshift.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Planetarium-style all-sky view synchronised with the ring and Penrose-strip animations.

historical_notes.event: Developed the conformal toolkit for classifying infinities and representing global causal structure, now drawn as Penrose diagrams.
historical_notes.significance: Made infinity and horizons tractable by geometry; underpins singularity theorems and black-hole physics, for which Penrose shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.

historical_notes.event: Co-credited in the alternative name Penrose-Carter diagrams; also contributed to the black-hole no-hair theorem and coined the term 'anthropic principle'.
historical_notes.significance: Signals that conformal diagrams were developed and popularised by more than one person, especially for black-hole spacetimes.

historical_notes.event: A famous Escher woodcut inspired the triangle-tiled Poincare disc image used in Fig. 19.3.
historical_notes.significance: Links a well-known artwork to the idea of a conformal map of an infinite space.

historical_notes.event: Exercise 19.8 follows Coleman's treatment of the closed dust universe, published in his collected relativity lectures (Coleman, 2022).
historical_notes.significance: Points readers to a pedagogical source for the cycloid parametrization and the light-round-the-universe timing.

applications_and_observations.topic: No horizons for an inertial observer in flat spacetime
applications_and_observations.details: Because all world lines begin at i- and the observer's endpoint i+ has everything in its past, an inertial Minkowski observer eventually receives signals from every event.

applications_and_observations.topic: Cosmological event horizon of a Lambda-dominated universe
applications_and_observations.details: Our estimate, not in the book: since the real Universe is approaching de Sitter behaviour, it inherits a future event horizon at proper distance about c/H_infinity with H_infinity = H0 sqrt(Omega_Lambda).
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our estimate: H0 about 68 km/s/Mpc and Omega_Lambda about 0.69 give H_infinity about 56 km/s/Mpc and c/H_infinity about 5.3 Gpc, roughly 17 billion light-years; galaxies beyond this will never be seen in their current state.

applications_and_observations.topic: Particle horizon in the Einstein-de Sitter model
applications_and_observations.details: Our estimate, not in the book: for a flat dust universe with a proportional to t^(2/3), the conformal-time light cone gives a particle horizon at proper distance 3ct.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our estimate: d_ph = 3ct; for t about 13.8 Gyr that is about 41 billion light-years in this idealised model (the Lambda-CDM value is about 46 billion light-years).

applications_and_observations.topic: Timeline of the closed dust Universe 6 in conformal time
applications_and_observations.details: Using the cycloid solution of Exercise 19.8: maximum expansion at eta = pi, Crunch at eta = 2 pi, and light covers comoving angle eta, so it reaches the antipode at maximum expansion and returns to its origin at the Crunch.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Our calculation from eqn 19.41: a_max = C at t = pi C/2; lifetime t = pi C.

applications_and_observations.topic: Red- and blueshift of multiple images in a recollapsing universe
applications_and_observations.details: An observer in a collapsing closed universe would see some direct images blueshifted while the long-way images of the same source are still redshifted, and near the Crunch most light is blueshifted, following omega a = const.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Signature (-,+,+,+); c = 1 throughout (and G = 1 in the Friedmann equation constants).

g-hat = Omega^2 g or g-bar = Omega^2 eta; in Exercise 19.3 the factor is written f(x). The physical line element is written ds^2 = (1/Omega^2) d-bar-s^2 for Minkowski but ds^2 = a^2 d-bar-s^2 and ds^2 = alpha^2 sec^2 t' d-bar-s^2 for cosmologies.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Watch which metric the factor multiplies.

notation_and_conventions.convention: g-hat denotes a generic conformally related metric; g-bar and d-bar-s the unphysical (rescaled) metric used for compactification.
i+ and i- future and past timelike infinity; i0 spacelike infinity; script I+ and script I- (pronounced 'scri plus/minus') future and past null infinity.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The OCR copy sometimes shows J^+ for script I. Figs 19.19-19.21 reuse scri- for the Big-Bang surface.

notation_and_conventions.convention: (t', r') for compactified Minkowski coordinates and t' for compactified time in de Sitter and Robertson-Walker diagrams; horizontal axis labelled r' for Minkowski and chi for cosmologies.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Example 19.6 drops primes in the scri line equations.

notation_and_conventions.convention: u = t - r (constant on outgoing rays), v = t + r (constant on incoming rays); v = tan p, u = tan q.
Sigma = sin chi (k = +1), chi (k = 0), sinh chi (k = -1); chi is the dimensionless comoving radial coordinate, 0 <= chi <= pi for k = 1.
tau in the text (dt = a dtau); eta in Exercise 19.8.
notation_and_conventions.notes: eta also denotes the Minkowski metric in the same chapter, and tau is proper time elsewhere in the book.

notation_and_conventions.convention: alpha = 1/H with H the constant Hubble rate.
Model universes carry the numbers assigned in Chapter 18: Universe 1 de Sitter, Universe 6 closed dust (k = 1, Lambda = 0), Universe 8 Einstein static.

Radial null rays at 45 degrees; each interior point represents a 2-sphere; spacelike singularities drawn as double lines; 'surfaces' refers to lines in the diagram because two dimensions are suppressed.
g(x, y) for the scalar product of vectors x and y, bold symbols for tensors.

margin_notes.summary: Two chapter epigraphs set a light tone about infinity: a line from the poet Alfred de Musset about being haunted by the infinite, and a garbled remark by the politician Dan Quayle about space being 'almost infinite'.
Boxed pointer: the chapter is mathematical, dealing with infinities, and can be skipped on a first reading by those keen to get on with the mechanics of relativity.
Timelike loops do occur in some places, for instance inside certain kinds of black hole, to be met later.
Biography of Roger Penrose, stressing his influence on singularity theory and black-hole physics and his 2020 Nobel Prize.
Conformal transformations are defined informally as those that locally preserve angles.
Boxed pointer that topology, the study of properties unchanged under deformation, is introduced in Appendix C.

Alternative name Penrose-Carter diagrams; biography of Brandon Carter with his work on the no-hair theorem (Chapter 29) and his naming of the anthropic principle, followed by a wry Penrose quotation explaining that principle.
Gives the metric definition of the cosine of the angle between two vectors (eqn 19.3), the formula that makes conformal angle-preservation evident.
Footnote 6 sends the reader to the exercises (Exercise 19.3) for the proof that angles and relative magnitudes survive a conformal rescaling.
Explains the pronunciation of script I as 'scri'.
Explains that the goal is a conformal map from Minkowski (t, r) to new coordinates (t', r') that turns the arrow picture into the Penrose triangle; the algebra is deferred a few pages.
Technically the construction extends Minkowski space by adding the points V = 0, to which the unphysical metric components (unlike eta) can be extended.
The cylinder picture of the Einstein universe corresponds to embedding x^2 + y^2 = 1 in 2+1 Minkowski space, and the full spacetime to a cylinder in 4+1 dimensions (Appendix D).
Global techniques are illustrated in Chapter 50; Penrose (1973) is recommended for the full account.
Footnote 12 says the algebra showing de Sitter space is conformal to a strip of the Einstein universe (eqn 19.23) is left to the exercises; it is Exercise 19.4.
Caution against thinking an observer at chi = pi/2 in de Sitter space sees the whole chi range sooner: homogeneity makes all positions equivalent and chi behaves like a radius.
Mnemonic: the future event horizon is the backward light cone cast from future infinity; the past event horizon is the forward cone cast from past infinity.
Lists Sigma(chi) for k = +1, 0, -1.
Gives the tanh-arctan transformation that makes the k = -1 metric conformal to part of the Einstein universe (printed with a sign error in r' and with t standing for conformal time).
Fig. 19.22 caption caution: do not confuse chi with the angle round the drawn circle, which differs by a factor of 2.

notable.summary: Take a uniformly moving particle in 1+1 Minkowski space, compute its velocity in light-cone coordinates, and explore what that 'velocity' does for different speeds.
notable.why_notable: Shows sharply that coordinate speeds can be misleading: a right-moving light ray is 'at rest' in u and a left-moving one has infinite speed.

notable.summary: Using the metric definition of the angle between vectors, show that multiplying the metric by a function leaves angles unchanged and keeps null curves null.
notable.why_notable: It is the one-line proof on which the whole chapter rests.

notable.summary: Starting from flat-slicing de Sitter, relate it to the five-dimensional hyperboloid, switch to global coordinates with closed spatial slices, then introduce a conformal time via a tangent-exponential relation to obtain the Einstein-strip form of eqn 19.23.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the derivation the text skips, and the flat-slicing map's w + v > 0 condition shows those coordinates cover only half of de Sitter.

notable.summary: Exploit the conformal invariance of electromagnetism in a Robertson-Walker universe: carry a plane-wave solution in conformal time back to cosmic time and deduce how frequency scales with the scale factor.
notable.why_notable: An elegant alternative derivation of cosmological redshift that uses the chapter's conformal idea physically.

notable.summary: Find the explicit relation between Minkowski (t, x) and Penrose (t', x') coordinates and use it to justify the shapes of the curves in Fig. 19.6.
notable.why_notable: The chapter never states t' +/- r' = 2 arctan(t +/- r); this exercise does and it is needed for any accurate plotting.

notable.summary: On the Minkowski Penrose diagram, draw the outgoing paths from the origin of a light pulse, a particle at 0.3 of light speed, and a spacelike curve with 'speed' 1.1.
notable.why_notable: Direct practice of the endpoint rules (i+, scri+, i0) and a natural target for an interactive plot.

notable.summary: Following Sidney Coleman, rewrite the closed dust Friedmann equation, identify conformal time with the comoving distance light travels, derive the cycloid solution for a and t in terms of it, and use this to check the observer's story in Example 19.10.
notable.why_notable: It quietly corrects the chapter's time ranges: the closed dust universe lasts 2 pi in conformal time, exactly one circuit for light.

exercises.solutions: Appendix E (Answers to selected problems) gives brief answers to 19.2(b), 19.3, 19.5, 19.6, 19.7 (with a figure) and 19.8.

difficulty.notes: Algebra is modest (trig identities, substitution into line elements) but the ideas are subtle: conformal rescaling, points at infinity, horizons defined over whole histories. The text is short and asserts key results (de Sitter compactification, k = -1 map, coordinate relations) without derivation, the figures carry much of the argument, and several printed slips (wrong sub-figure reference, sign error in margin note 16, t' = -pi/2 for future infinity, sin^2 phi in 19.37, time ranges in Example 19.9) can derail a careful reader. The authors themselves mark the chapter as skippable.

teaching_gems.gem: Point arrows at the five infinities on an ordinary t-r plot, then show the finished Penrose triangle before any algebra.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners know what the mathematics must produce, so the compactification reads as achieving a visible goal rather than a sequence of substitutions.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Two-panel scene: fire timelike, null and spacelike curves from the origin on the left; each lands on a glowing boundary piece of the triangle on the right.

teaching_gems.gem: Deliberately fail first: V = 1/v puts infinity at V = 0 but the metric blows up, so a conformal factor is needed.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The failure motivates the unphysical metric and makes clear that coordinate changes alone cannot tame infinity.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Symbolic stepper where the learner tries V = 1/v, sees the coefficient plot diverge at V = 0, then applies Omega = V and watches it flatten.

teaching_gems.gem: Use the arctangent graph as the entire intuition for compactification.
teaching_gems.why_effective: One familiar function captures how an infinite range becomes finite, and explains why grid lines crowd near the edges.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Grid-morph animation driven by a slider that blends x into arctan x for both null coordinates.

teaching_gems.gem: Paint every spacetime as a patch on the same Einstein static cylinder.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A single canvas turns abstract comparisons (Minkowski vs de Sitter vs Big-Bang models) into visibly different shapes, and makes 'boundary of the patch = infinity or singularity' concrete.
teaching_gems.app_idea: 3D cylinder with a spacetime picker; patches animate in and a button unrolls the chosen patch into its Penrose diagram.

teaching_gems.gem: Read horizons straight off the boundary shape: a point-like past infinity means no particle horizon; a spacelike past boundary means one exists; a point-like future endpoint means no event horizon.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives learners a quick diagnostic rule that transfers to black holes and any new spacetime.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Quiz mode: a random Penrose diagram appears and the learner predicts particle/event horizons before the observer tool reveals them.

teaching_gems.gem: Mnemonic for event horizons: sit at future infinity and cast a backward cone; sit at past infinity and cast a forward cone.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Compresses two definitions into one symmetric action that is easy to perform on any diagram.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Draggable 'lamp' that can be dropped on scri+ or scri-; it casts the corresponding cone and labels it future or past event horizon.

teaching_gems.gem: Classify events around a world line as seen-and-influenced, influenced-only, seen-only.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Separates two questions novices conflate (can I see it? can I affect it?) and shows each has its own horizon.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Colour-coded region map with a click-to-query event tool.

teaching_gems.gem: Tell the life of a closed universe from the observer's sky: more stars, all stars, duplicate stars, then the back of your own head at the Crunch, with red- turning to blueshift.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A memorable narrative that exercises light-cone reasoning, closed topology and redshift in one story, and checks the diagram against intuition.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Synchronised ring-universe, Penrose-strip and all-sky views driven by one time slider.

teaching_gems.gem: Introduce conformal invariance with a familiar Riemannian image, the Poincare disc.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners see angle preservation and size distortion in a picture they may already know before meeting it in Lorentzian form.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Drag a fixed-size hyperbolic triangle toward the rim, then switch to dragging a light cone toward scri.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed text on p.205 says constant-t (spacelike) lines map to the curves of Fig. 19.6(a); they are in Fig. 19.6(b).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A reader comparing text and figure will think the timelike and spacelike families coincide.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Refer to 19.6(a) for constant r and 19.6(b) for constant t; in the app, colour-code the two families.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 19.6 caption says the curves are for r' and t' = 0.5 ... 2.5, but they are images of constant Minkowski r and t, and the explicit map t' +/- r' = 2 arctan(t +/- r) is never given in the text (only in Appendix E).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners cannot reproduce the figure or check its curves.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State the explicit map when introducing the triangle and label curves by Minkowski r and t values.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin note 16 prints the k = -1 transformation with a plus sign in both t' and r' (so r' = t'), and writes t where the conformal time tau is meant. The r' expression needs a minus sign.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Anyone attempting to verify the k = -1 mapping gets a degenerate transformation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use t' +/- r' = 2 arctan tanh[(tau +/- chi)/2]; verify that the static open metric becomes cosh(tau+chi) cosh(tau-chi) times the Einstein metric.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: In the de Sitter discussion the bracketed remark gives future infinity as t' = -pi/2; future infinity is t' = +pi/2. The same remark blurs that the observer's final past cone reaches all chi only at the bottom edge (scri-, t' = -pi/2).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confuses which edge is future infinity and why every galaxy is glimpsed yet some events are never seen.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say: at t' = pi/2 the past cone of the chi = 0 observer reaches chi = pi exactly at t' = -pi/2, so every comoving world line is seen at early times, but the upper-right triangle lies beyond the event horizon.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 19.22 uses flat-slicing de Sitter (Universe 1), but those coordinates cover only half of the de Sitter hyperboloid (w + v > 0, the triangle t' > chi - pi/2 in the square). The square diagram and eqn 19.23 belong to the global cosh slicing of Exercise 19.4(b). Eqn 19.22 also prints ds for ds^2, and the Einstein coordinates are listed with r instead of chi.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think the exponentially expanding flat universe fills the whole square, obscuring that its past boundary is a null horizon, not scri-.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Draw the full square for global de Sitter and shade the flat-slicing half; connect with Chapter 18's exercise that these coordinates cover half the hyperboloid.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 19.37 in Exercise 19.4(b) prints sin^2 phi where sin^2 chi is required.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Stalls the exercise for readers checking their result.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Correct to alpha^2 cosh^2(t/alpha)[dchi^2 + sin^2 chi dOmega^2].

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 19.9 says conformal time for the k = 1 dust model runs from 0 to infinity and maps to t' from 0 to pi; for closed dust it actually runs from 0 to 2 pi (Exercise 19.8's own cycloid). The book's square k = 1 diagram with chi = 0 identified with chi = pi is therefore a half-scale picture of one great circle, not the literal 3-sphere coordinates in which chi = 0 and chi = pi are antipodes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers who combine Sigma = sin chi with the identification get contradictions about antipodal points and about when light returns.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present the accurate diagram (width pi, height 2 pi, rays reflecting through the poles) and, if the ring picture is used, define psi = 2 chi as the angle round a great circle.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 19.9 calls the k = 0 region 'diamond-shaped' with 0 < t < pi; it is the upper half-triangle of the Minkowski diagram (0 < t' < pi), as Figs 19.18 and 19.19 show.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Mismatch between text and figure about the patch shape.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Describe it as Minkowski's Penrose triangle cut along t' = 0.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Figures 19.19-19.21 label the Big-Bang singular edge as scri-, and the text says timelike geodesics start 'on scri-'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Conflates past null infinity (infinitely far) with a singularity a finite time in the past, undermining the chapter's own closing distinction.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Label the edge 'Big Bang (spacelike singularity)' and reserve scri for genuine null or conformal infinity.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The claim that flat and open dust universes have a past event horizon is unusual terminology; standard treatments (Rindler) say these models have particle horizons but no event horizons.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners reading other sources will find conflicting statements.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Explain that with a spacelike initial singularity, an observer's early influence region is limited (the book's 'past event horizon'), and that other texts describe this situation as the existence of particle horizons.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: No warning that conformal rescaling changes curvature and timelike geodesics: the unphysical partner of Minkowski is the curved Einstein universe, and only null geodesics carry over.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may try to read particle orbits or tidal effects off the unphysical metric.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a quick check: compute the Ricci scalar of the Einstein static metric (6, nonzero) versus 0 for Minkowski.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 19.6 writes the scri lines with unprimed t + r = pi and t - r = -pi.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Minor confusion between Minkowski and compactified coordinates.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Fig. 19.17's side triangles (neither seen nor influenced) are not labelled or discussed, and the rectangle's aspect ratio is not explained.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may assume regions I-III exhaust spacetime.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add region IV explicitly and draw the observer's endpoints on the edges of the de Sitter square.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The symbol eta means the Minkowski metric in Section 19.1 and conformal time in Exercise 19.8; tau is conformal time here but proper time elsewhere in the book.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Notation collisions when moving between chapters.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Causal past and future sets, and the precise definitions of particle and event horizons (via comoving world lines and the observer's endpoint), are given only through pictures.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Hard to apply the ideas to a new spacetime without a formal handle.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Supplement with the conformal-time formulas: particle horizon radius chi = tau - tau_initial and event horizon radius chi = tau_final - tau.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'If you waited forever, could you eventually receive a light signal from every galaxy?' Let the learner guess, then promise a drawing that answers it for any universe.

Before any formulas, have the learner list where a curve can 'go to infinity' on a t-r plot: straight up, straight down, sideways, and along the two light-ray diagonals. Then name i+, i-, i0, scri+ and scri-.
Teach conformal invariance in one line: multiply every inner product by the same positive number and a zero stays zero. Check: 'Does rescaling change which vectors are null? Does it change lengths?'

Sequence the construction as: null coordinates, arctan squashing, spot the divergent overall factor, divide it out, recognise the Einstein universe. Use the failed V = 1/v attempt to justify step four.
Always pair the Penrose triangle with the explicit map t' +/- r' = 2 arctan(t +/- r); the chapter omits it and learners need it to plot anything.

Understanding check: ask the learner to place, on the Minkowski triangle, the world line of a particle moving at 0.3c from the origin (ends at i+), a light pulse (ends on scri+), and a constant-time slice (ends at i0).

When moving to de Sitter, ask what changed about the boundary (edges became horizontal, i.e. spacelike) before discussing horizons; then let the learner discover that a past cone no longer reaches the whole bottom edge.

Distinguish horizons explicitly: particle horizon = which galaxies have I seen at least once so far; event horizon = which events will I ever see. Ask for a case with one but not the other (Einstein-de Sitter: particle horizon, no event horizon).

Correct the printed slips proactively if the learner reads the book: Fig. 19.6(b) for spatial slices, t' = +pi/2 for de Sitter future infinity, the minus sign in margin note 16's r', sin^2 chi in eqn 19.37.

For the closed universe, work in conformal time with the cycloid a = (C/2)(1 - cos eta): maximum expansion at eta = pi, crunch at 2 pi. Explain the book's square diagram as a half-scale great-circle picture to avoid the antipode confusion.

Common learner question: 'Is the Big Bang the same as past infinity since it is at the bottom edge?' Answer: both are edges, but the Big Bang is a finite proper time away and is a singularity; the diagram hides that distinction unless you label it.
Common learner question: 'Do Penrose diagrams tell me how far away things are?' No; only causal relations and null directions are faithful. Use the Poincare disc to show why.
Link forward: the future event horizon in de Sitter is the template for the black-hole event horizon; the Big-Bang spacelike singularity foreshadows the singularity inside a Schwarzschild black hole.
